Massif is a map editor for Minecraft Java worlds in the spirit of WorldPainter, with a node-based terrain generator in the spirit of Gaea, written in Rust.

## New in 1.1.1

## New in 1.1.0

**Work on one map together (beta)**

Several people can now work on the same map and join their work. The owner keeps the map; contributors start from one of its versions and send their changes back as a small `.massifpatch` file (Versions ▸ Export my changes…), only the tiles they changed: about 2 MB for 1,000 × 1,000 blocks reshaped on a real map. The owner brings it in (Import a contribution…) and reviews it on the map: the changed areas drawn over the 2D map, new, changed or in conflict where both changed the same land, each accepted or rejected, a conflict settled with mine, theirs or tile by tile, the settings of the map it changes switched on one by one. Applying it is one step to undo and a new version. A zone sent to World Machine or Gaea comes back the same way: Export Region keeps a version and writes zone.json beside the images, and the images brought back are compared with that version and reviewed before anything changes. A shared folder (Google Drive, Dropbox, iCloud, Git) can hold the published map and the contributions, so that nobody sends files by hand. Save points are now the map's versions: each shows who made it, the one the map stands on and the merges. A part of a big map can go to someone as a map of its own: File ▸ Export Region… as a Massif map writes the selection and a border of tiles around it, at its place, with the map's terrains, layers and versions; File ▸ Merge Massif Map… brings their work back, with the map shown before and after, the changed tiles outlined, conflicts marked, each area accepted or rejected, and the terrains and layers they made added to the map.

**Tools for WorldPainter terraformers**

The Info panel is now WorldPainter's inspector: it follows the cursor over the 2D map and the 3D view and shows the column's coordinates, height, water, terrain, biome (painted or automatic), whether it is selected, and every layer painted there — cover, trees, under the trees, tree size, pockets, smoothed steps, combined layers, annotation — with its intensity; the world's name, seed, sea level, spawn, blocks, size and memory moved to File ▸ World Information…. A stroke all outside the selection now says why nothing happens. Brush filters can be on layers too (ferns, tall grass, tree and object layers, pockets, annotations), their list is searchable and sorted with what the map holds first, by recent use or A–Z, and an eyedropper picks what the filter is on by clicking the map or the 3D view. Right-click a layer ▸ Find takes the map to the nearest place it is painted, then the next. The new Pencil (Brush Settings) draws an unbroken hard line that follows the mouse, one block wide and joined by the blocks' sides, with any tool. Alt and the wheel turn the brush, as in WorldPainter, and Ctrl and the wheel zoom. The map's grid shows the region files' borders (512 blocks) with their names, r.x.z.mca, for merging maps, and Test Export can pick whole regions on the map, or round any part out to them, listing the region files it writes.

**Palettes, every object setting of WorldPainter, and tree sizes of your own**

Layers sort into **palettes**, as in WorldPainter: named groups at the top of the Layers panel that fold, rename and move, holding layers of any kind; drag a layer onto one, or use Palette in its menu, and a palette deleted sends its layers back to their sections. Your brush groups work the same way: fold them, rename or delete them, drag a brush to another. A WorldPainter world or layer file keeps its palettes. An object layer now lists its objects in a compact list: click one to edit it, Shift+Click, Shift+Arrows or Cmd/Ctrl+Click to edit several at once, with each object's frequency, origin and, with Own rules, every attribute of WorldPainter's object dialog — turned and mirrored at random or fixed, raised and varied in height or at a fixed height, on land, on air, under or on water and lava, what it collides with and replaces underground, its leaves, waterlogging, joined fences and a block placed as air; WorldPainter's objects come in with all of them. **Tree sizes** are yours to define: add sizes such as Tiny, Forest or Open-grown, set each object's size by hand (Auto still guesses from its height), and give each size its own density in a layer's settings. Trees can now be spaced **by canopy**: Massif measures each tree's crown from its leaves (or takes the radius you set), and two neighbours stand as far apart as their crowns need, so that crowns touch without overlapping and narrow trees no longer stand as far apart as broad ones; a least gap keeps trunks apart. Layers of objects you import are spaced by canopy; older layers keep their grid until you switch them.

**True Colour view**

The 2D map and the 3D views have a new mode, True Colour, that shows the map as it will look in the game once exported rather than in Massif's editor colours: every block in its texture's colour, and grass, leaves, vines and water tinted by the biome they stand in, as the game does (a River biome no longer makes grass blue). Resource packs added in the Blocks panel change these colours in their order, the last one winning as in the game, including OptiFine's custom colour maps for grass, leaves and any block they name; mods' blocks show in their own textures' colours. The Render side tints its blocks with the same colour maps. Asked for by Jack (Fornad).

**KubeJS blocks and connected textures from modpacks.** Reading an instance (**Use** in the Blocks panel, or **Instance…**) now also reads the blocks its KubeJS scripts make, listed as a mod named KubeJS: the blocks its startup scripts register, with the names, shapes and textures the scripts give them, and the states, models and textures written in its `kubejs/assets` folder; a resource pack left as a folder, given to **Add mods…**, reads too. Connected textures made for Fusion or OptiFine (CTM, read by Continuity too) show as in the game: each block shows one tile at its real size in the Blocks panel (Fusion's sheets were drawn whole on each block, shrunk eight times), and in the True Colour view each top shows the tiles its neighbours give it. Thanks to nicolas-vinc, who wrote the reading of KubeJS's folder and of Fusion's sheets.

**Annotations in any colour, with their opacity, drawn as curves; sharper contour lines**

Annotations now show in the 3D views too, and an eye in the Annotations tool's settings (also the pen button in the map's header, and View ▸ Show Annotations) shows or hides them all at once; each colour has its own opacity in the tool's settings. Besides WorldPainter's fifteen colours, the Colour button picks any colour, which the map keeps with its own. The Annotations tool can also draw curves, as Axiom's Path tool: click points on the map, move them, add or take some off, and pick a smooth curve through every point, Bézier handles or straight lines, with a width at its start and another at its end; it shows as the ribbon it will paint until you press Enter, then becomes an annotation like any other. The contour lines are now WorldPainter's: a solid dark line every 10 blocks and a finer one halfway, readable at every zoom; the arrow beside their button sets the interval (5, 10, 20, 50 or any), their strength, black or white lines, crisp or smooth edges.

**World rules in the export: no more /gamerule after each export**

The export dialog has a Rules tab: the game mode, the difficulty, and the world's game rules, written into the world so that it opens as set. Pick a preset, Creative / Frozen (nothing spawns, spreads, grows or decays, no weather nor day going by, noon for good: to walk round a map as it was built), Survival safe (fire does not spread, mobs break no blocks) or Vanilla, or set each rule: mobs, pillager patrols, the wandering trader, phantoms, mobs changing blocks, fire spreading, random ticks, keeping one's inventory, the day and the weather going by, the time of day and the weather. Save a set of rules under your own name with Save as preset… (Settings ▸ Export lists them), and each map keeps the rules of its last export. They are written as each version of Minecraft names them, the new names of 1.21.11 and the file of their own of 26.1 included.

**Smoother brushes, and a performance recorder**

Painting and sculpting with a large brush no longer drags the whole window down when the Diorama or the Render side is open: those views now rebuild what a stroke changed a few times a second and on their own threads, instead of compressing the edited tiles and taking the brush's own processor time every frame, and raising land no longer looks for water to fill at each touch of the brush. On a 4,096-block map with a 100-block brush, a stroke took a third of the processor time it took before. When Massif still stutters, **Help ▸ Record Performance…** records it: start it, do what is slow, click the red dot at the top right to stop, and a `.zip` lands on your desktop with every frame and where its time went, your computer and settings, the map's size and what you did, never the map itself, to send us in #bug-reports.

**WorldPainter's overlay images come with the world.** Importing a `.world` brings the surface's overlay images (WorldPainter's View ▸ Overlays) as reference images of the map, at the same place, scale and opacity, shown or hidden as they were. Their files are looked for where WorldPainter had them, then by name beside the `.world`, so a world made on Windows finds its pictures on a Mac when they travel with it. One that is not found keeps its place and is named in the import report; **Find its file…**, in the reference image's settings, links it again.

**Layers laid over the land as WorldPainter ground covers can become the land itself.** A WorldPainter map made for Conquest Reforged often lays a block's layers over the land as a custom ground cover (`grass_block_layer` over grass, snow layers): imported, the land stood a block lower than it looked, and Massif's tools did not know its height. The import report now lists those covers, ticked; **Make them the ground's own** raises each column by its layers' eighths, puts the full block on top (keeping the terrain when it already is that block) and smooths it with layers on export, so the exported world looks as before while the map, the 3D view, the brushes and Smooth terrain follow the land's true height. Untick a cover to keep it a cover; it is one step to undo.

**Linked map sizes, snowfall, noise gradients**

The width and depth of a new map, of a new world from a real place and of a map resized are linked by a chain: typing one sets the other, until you click the chain to set them apart. Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Snowfall… lays snow as the wind and the slopes leave it — drifts in the lee of ridges and in hollows, bare windward slopes, none on steep cliffs or over water —, in snow layers then snow blocks, within a band of heights, with a preview first and one step to undo. Noise painting has a Blend that turns its list into an ordered gradient (dirt, then coarse dirt, then grass, dithered between neighbours), and the same mix is the terrain graph's new Noise paint node, which shares its presets with the brush.

**Every typeface fits the smallest window.** In Inter, Geist, IBM Plex Sans or Manrope (Settings ▸ Typeface), a few things took more room than the narrowest sidebar or the smallest window gave them: the selection tools' Invert folded onto two lines in Russian, the links under a new map ran past the window's edge in French, and Export Region grew taller than a window of 640 points, its buttons scrolling out of view with the rest. The selection tools' buttons now go to the next line whole, the links take a second line when they need one, and Export Region's settings scroll under buttons that stay in view.

## New in 1.0.0

**The Gradient brush is easy to find.** It sat in the Paint row behind an icon of two circles that said little. It now has an icon of its own, a swatch fading from full to empty, marked with a dot until you first try it, and its card says it is new. Paint terrain's Tool Settings also offer it as a third way to paint, beside **One terrain** and **Noise**, and the Gradient brush shows the same choice to go back. The tour and the help point to it.

**Unpainting gives back the map's own terrain.** The right button of Paint terrain used to put back the terrain the height calls for, so on a map filled with rock, unpainting a high place turned it to snow. It now puts back the map's own terrain: the one a new map was filled with, or, on a map made before, the one covering nearly all of it. Tool Settings shows which under **Right button**, where **Change** picks another and **By height** brings back the old way, which maps made from their height keep. 3D Sculpt's Paint does the same.

**Frames a second without vsync, for developers.** **Settings ▸ Developer** now has **Frames a second**: **Vsync** keeps the window in step with the screen as before, while 60, 120, 144, 240 or **Unlimited** show each frame as soon as it is drawn, up to that number. **Draw every frame** keeps the window drawing even when nothing changes, so the Developer panel's charts show how many frames your computer makes. Both apply at once and only while developer mode is on.

**The right button no longer upsets the player's view.** In 3D Sculpt as the player, with the mouse held by the view, pressing the right button could let the hidden pointer go: it wandered off the view onto the panels around, or out of the window, and the view lost hold of the mouse. While the view holds the mouse, the pointer now stays at the crosshair whatever the system reports, so both buttons always use the tool there, and on macOS the pointer is never moved behind your back (which undid the lock).

**Speckled custom brushes draw a clean outline.** A custom brush made of many specks (THIJS BRUSHES, WorldPainter's noise and cracked earth…) drew its outline over the map as long straight lines shooting across it from the brush, in a tangle of pieces: its specks smaller than a pixel made loops that turned back on themselves, and the lines' corners shot far away. The outline is now traced at the size it is drawn: specks too small to see merge into the shapes they make, and a few hundred loops at most are drawn, in the 2D map as in the 3D views. Of 32 brushes tried (the 14 of THIJS BRUSHES, WorldPainter's 16 and the two it ships with), 18 drew stray lines at some size; none does now.

**A cleaner crosshair, and your choice of it.** The crosshair of the player's view is now a thin cross around an open middle, white in a soft dark outline, so it shows on snow as on deep water. **Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ Crosshair** offers a **Dot**, the **Cross**, a **Circle**, Minecraft's plus or **None**, with its size and opacity, beside a preview on light ground and dark.

**A calmer 3D view far off.** Far off, the small waves of the water made rings of moiré and the steps of grassy slopes turned into brown stair-stepped stripes. The waves now fade out where they get finer than a pixel and the sun's glint softens with them; the side of a block narrower than a pixel blends into the colour of the tops around it, as do the shading of block corners and the slight differences from block to block; and the game's textures are smoothed along faces seen edge-on. With **Smooth edges** on (Medium and High), once the view has been still for a moment, the ground is drawn once more with four rays a pixel, so the edges of its steps are smoothed as the water's already were. That one frame takes about twice as long (13 ms instead of 5 to 6 at 1,600 × 1,000 on an M4); a moving view and Low cost what they did.

**Auto biome shows what it leaves as it is.** Hovered over the map, Auto biome and Auto paint colour only the columns they would change, so a brush half over land that already had the biome it calls for (painted by an earlier stroke, say) seemed to paint only half of its outline, and in the map's Terrain mode the biomes painted do not show at all. The part of the brush left as it is is now hatched, and a bar under the map names what the columns become, with their colours, and how much of the brush already has what the land calls for; the tool's hint says that biomes show in the map's **Biome** mode. A custom brush turned toward 45° also showed the corners past its radius as left alone (up to 2 % of the brush) though a stroke changed them: the preview works them out too.

**The Gradient brush: terrains that blend instead of meeting on a line.** A new tool in the Paint tools, asked for by the Conquest Reforged and ArdaCraft terraformers. Paint the base terrains first — patches of rock in grass, a dark pit — then drag the Gradient brush over the edge: the rock gives way to a rim of other blocks, then to grass, as on a real hillside. A gradient is your terrains (or terrain mixes, or any block of the game or of your mods, Conquest Reforged's included) in bands of so many blocks, with between each two a hard cut, a ragged noise or blobs of every size going into each other, and a midpoint that sets how far each goes into the other. **Wander** makes a rim wide here and thin there instead of an even outline. Build and save your own in its editor, as in a picture editor's gradient: presets to start from, the bands with their real textures on a bar, stops to drag (a click adds one), diamonds for the midpoints, a marker for where the edge falls, each transition's kind, intensity and size, and a live preview of the result. It lays the gradient by distance to the edge between two terrains, or from the edge of the selection, or from the brush's centre for a patch with rings; it keeps to the selection, the filters, the intensity and soft edges, and a stroke is one step to undo. The map keeps the gradients it is painted with, and gradients are shared in `.massifpack` files with the terrains they need. Four built-in gradients are a start: Rock to grass, Pit to grass, Deciduous forest to grass and Shore.

**Waterfalls down steep slopes.** A river dug with the River tool or Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Rivers used to go down a steep slope as a trench whose water stepped down a block every few blocks. Where the land is steep, it now falls from pool to pool: its water stays level in a pool dug into the slope, then falls two to five blocks into the next one (the steeper the slope, the higher the falls), with a plunge pool dug under each fall. On gentler ground it still steps down a block at a time, like rapids, and through a lake on its way it keeps the lake's level. In the game, each fall is a curtain of falling water that stays as it is.

**A real place brought into a map is painted from its own relief.** **Edit ▸ Relief of a Real Place…** into an existing map used to keep the old map's painted terrains: patches of sand from a map of waste ground lay at random spots on the new land. The land is now painted from the new relief, as a new world from a real place is (sand along the water only, rock on cliffs, snow above the snow line), and the biomes, ground covers and objects painted there are taken off, so the automatic biomes follow the new land. **Terrains ▸ Keep** in the dialog keeps your paint and writes only the heights and the water.

**The water tools work at any height.** Flood and the Water brush used to lay water only up to the water level of Tool Settings, the sea's (63) to begin with, so above the sea they did nothing, and Flood only said "Nothing to fill or drain here". Now they work wherever you use them. Flood fills the hollow you click up to the lowest point of its rim, where the water would spill, and the Water brush lays water as high as where each stroke starts: the surface of the water there, or a block over the ground. **From the click**, in Tool Settings, turns this off to use a level of your own. A limit is now an option, off by default: **Limit the water's height** keeps the water under a height of your choice, such as the sea's. When nothing fills, the message says why and how to change it.

**Choose the map's size when you bring in a real place.** **Edit ▸ Relief of a Real Place…** over the whole map replaces its land anyway, so the dialog now lets you change the map's size at the same time: keep it, or type a new width and depth (made whole tiles of 128 blocks, up to 32,768 a side). The map is cut or grown around its middle and the place fills all of it. The dialog says clearly that the land is replaced, what happens to your painted biomes, covers, objects, levels and sculptures (kept inside the new size, gone outside it), about how much memory the new size takes, and warns when it will be slow or may not fit in your computer's memory. It is all one step: undo brings the old map back, size and all.

**Water that stays where you put it in the game.** Minecraft leaves the water of an exported world still until a block next to it changes; then every step of a river runs over into the pool below, two sources side by side make new ones, and pool after pool rises until the water overflows its banks. On a WorldPainter map of 5,888 blocks a side with its rivers and lakes, nearly 400,000 blocks of water would appear that way, 157,000 of them over dry land. The export now writes the water as the game would leave it: a row of flowing water at the edge of each step, falling water where it drops, and, where a new source would form, flowing water instead of the sources beside it. Worked out with the game's own rules over every water block of that map, nothing moves any more once updated. Rivers dug with the River tool or Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Rivers keep their water in their bed: a bank dug lower than the water beside it rises back to hold it, or the river's own water goes down to the bank, and water already on the map is never lowered. Blocks of objects standing in water (fences, slabs, leaves…) are written waterlogged. Water you painted over lower land, on a slope, now runs down it in the export, as it would in the game. The export of that map takes a second or two longer.

**A sharp 2D map, block by block.** Close up, the 2D map is shaded from each block's height as the game will build it, the way the game's own maps are: every step of a block is a crisp line one block wide, lit where it faces the light and in shadow at its foot, the contour lines follow the blocks, and the height of each block reads at a glance, as in WorldPainter. Before, the shading followed the smooth shape of the ground under the blocks, so a map imported from WorldPainter or shaped with soft brushes looked blurred and its steps disappeared. **Block steps**, a new button in the map's header next to the contour lines, turns back to the smooth shading if you prefer it. Zoomed out, the map is drawn as before, as quickly and with the same memory.

**A roomier node search.** The node library of the Terrain graph (Tab or right-click) is now a large picker that stays inside the window wherever it opens: a dozen results at once, grouped by family, with the chosen node's description under the list. Type part of a name in your language, in English or in any language Massif speaks, or just its letters in order (`thrml` finds Thermal erosion); ↑ and ↓ choose, Enter adds, Esc closes. With nothing typed, the nodes you added last come first.

**Worlds open in every version without being converted.** An export for Minecraft 1.19 to 26.3 now also writes the world's settings as that version does: the spawn point and the border as 1.21.9 keeps them, and for 26.1 and later the world's folders as 26.1 lays them out, with its generation, weather, time of day and border in files of their own. The game opens the world as it is, with no question about making a backup and nothing converted. Worlds exported for 26.3 also name their blocks as 26.3 reads them, where they used to come out wrong in that version. Worlds exported for 1.20 to 1.21.11 now carry the state of the fight with the Ender Dragon, as a new world of the game does, so the game no longer writes an error about it in its log each time it starts them.

**Blocks from mods: Conquest Reforged and others.** The Blocks panel has a new **Mods** row: **Add mods…** reads the jars of mods with blocks from the `mods` folder of your instance (Conquest Reforged, Chipped, Macaw's…, made for Forge, NeoForge, Fabric or Quilt). Their blocks appear beside the game's, in sections named after each mod, with their real textures and colours; you paint them, make terrains of them or grow them as covers like any other block, and the export writes them under their own names, ready for the game with the same mods installed. Massif remembers the mods you added, and a jar that cannot be read is named rather than stopping the others. Resource packs (`.zip`) go in the same list, after the mods, for those whose textures come apart, as Conquest Reforged's can: a pack's textures replace its mod's.

**Conquest Reforged, ready in one click.** Where Conquest Reforged is installed (CurseForge, Prism, Modrinth or the official launcher), the Blocks panel now offers it: **Use** reads its instance at once, over Minecraft 1.20.1, the version it plays. Its 17,020 blocks all show with their real textures and names, in its own 36 creative tabs (Cobble and Brick, Advanced Masonry, Columns, Roofing…), and **All shapes** adds each block's slabs, stairs, arches, capitals and other shapes after it. Massif also reads the list Conquest writes for WorldPainter users, `conquest_wp.csv`, from the instance or from WorldPainter's own folder, so you find the same palette: with it, the 79 files of the mod that are no blocks of the game are left out, and every block keeps the states the game gives it. Conquest's tall plants grow in their two halves, its plants grow on its own grass, moss, forest floors and soils, and objects made of its shaped blocks keep valid states when they are turned or mirrored. The export picks 1.20.1 and the instance's saves folder by itself when your map uses Conquest's blocks, and warns in red if you choose another version or if a mod's blocks are not read. A test map painted with 150 of its blocks, exported and read back with an independent reader, holds only block states that exist in the game. Reading the 222 MB mod takes about half a second, five times faster than before, with a third of the memory at its peak. **Instance…** reads any other modpack the same way. With both of Conquest's modpacks installed, Fabric and Forge, each is offered on its own row; Conquest Reforged 1.7.0 for Forge reads too, with its 18,249 blocks.

**Your WorldPainter layers come with your map.** Importing a `.world` used to keep only its land, terrains, water and biomes, and to list every layer as "not imported yet". Now the layers WorldPainter map makers paint most come along: forests (Deciduous, Pine, Jungle, Swamp) and the trees of WorldPainter Modernised's tree pack become object layers of the same trees, as dense as you painted them; your own custom object layers become object layers with their objects read from the world itself (Sponge and MCEdit schematics, structures, Bo2), keeping their offset, frequency and random turn; plant layers become ground covers with the same plants in the same shares; Frost, Lava, Void and Annotations come in too. On a WorldPainter map of 5,888 blocks a side, every layer now comes in (Grass and flowers, Big oaks, Birches, Cherry trees, Flowers, Tall grass, Dead trees, Firs, Tall spruces, Frost), in the same second the import took before. The import report says what became what, and lists the few layers left (caverns and chasms, tunnels, custom ground cover and combined layers).

**Frost, Lava and Annotations, as in WorldPainter.** Every new map has a **Frost** cover, which lays snow on the ground and turns the top of the water to ice, and a **Lava** cover, which turns the water where you paint it into lava; any cover can do the same (**The water**: As it is, Frozen or Lava, in its settings), and older maps find both in Packs. The new **Annotations** tool (Paint group, and fifteen colours at the bottom of the Layers panel) marks the map in colour to plan it, as WorldPainter's annotations do: drawn over the map, never exported, rubbed out with the right button, hidden with the pen button of the map's header.

**Clearer tool icons.** The tools have new icons, drawn in the style of the rest of the interface: one line weight, round ends, and the picture you would expect — a paintbrush to paint, a pipette to pick, a pickaxe and a shovel to sculpt and dig, a mound and an arrow to raise the land, a level pressed down to flatten it, a road, waves for rivers, a basin for flooding, a floating island for levels. They stay sharp at every size and on every screen. If you prefer the icons of the earlier versions, **Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ Tool icons** offers them as **Classic**.

**Massif in Spanish and Portuguese.** **Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ Language** now also offers Español and Português, and Massif picks them by itself on a Spanish or Portuguese system. The whole interface is translated, in the words Minecraft players use in those languages; the Portuguese is written for Brazil. The help and the online guide stay in English for now. A few choices in Settings that stayed in English in 0.6.0 (the theme's System, the sounds' Off, the notifications' Never, the memory's Automatic) are translated too, and the section titles of the Layers panel no longer run under their button in a narrow panel or a longer language.

**Your work is safer.** Saving never harms the file already there: Massif writes the new one beside it and puts it in place only once it is whole and on the disk, so a full disk, a folder that cannot be written, or a file that OneDrive, an antivirus or a backup tool is holding leaves the old file as it was, and the message says which it was and what to do. Exports, packs, height maps, images and Massif's own settings are written the same way. Should Massif run into an error while you work, it no longer closes: it writes a copy of your map at once and offers **Save As…**, **Carry On** or **Quit**, and a copy kept when you quit is offered back at the next start; an error in a task in the background only stops that task. Maps sculpted in 3D over thousands of chunks, or holding large libraries of objects, could be saved but not opened again: they open now. Damaged or hostile files (schematics, packs, height maps, GeoTIFFs, WorldPainter worlds, Massif maps) are refused with a message instead of closing Massif or filling its memory. Huge maps take half the memory to open (1.2 GB instead of 2.3 GB for a map of 44,544 × 33,536 blocks), and the steps to undo are kept within a gigabyte, the oldest let go first.

**A guided tour for your first map, and samples to explore.** The first time a map is open, a short tour of six steps shows the window: the World and Terrain sides, the tools, Brush Settings, the 2D map, the 3D view, and saving and exporting. Each step dims the window except for the part it talks about and says a few words beside it. **Next** and **Back** (or the arrow keys) move through it, and **Skip tour** or Esc ends it at any step. It does not come back on its own, and Massif shows no other tips or popups; **Help ▸ Take the tour** shows it again. If you used Massif before this version, it does not show by itself. The home screen also has **Samples**: Alpine range, Archipelago and Floating mountains, small maps of 768 blocks a side that open in one click. Each is made from a template of the terrain generator when you open it, in a few seconds, so Massif ships no extra files for them.

**Cleaner real places, up to 32,768 blocks.** A new world from a real place no longer ends in stretched stripes along its east and south edges: it is read to its last column from the data, the area rounded up to whole tiles. Lone spikes and pits a pixel wide, and the gaps of the data, are filled from the heights around them instead of standing up as needles or sinking as holes. The sea, which the data often gives as 0 m flat, is now water rather than dry ground level with it. The ground is painted from the real place, so the biomes follow the land: sand lies along the water only, not over every low field (which then read as deserts), and snow only above the snow line of the latitude, not on a hill that the scale makes tall. A new world can be up to 32,768 blocks a side (16,384 before): about two minutes and 600 MB of memory to make.

**Massif opens again when a recent map has a long name.** Since 0.3.1, which brought the home screen, a map in the list of recent maps whose name was too long for the home screen's side bar (more likely in a smaller window, or with Windows' display scaling at 125 or 150 %) froze Massif on its very first frame: the window stayed white and Windows called it "not responding". Long names are now cut with an ellipsis as they should be. Starting is also lighter on slower PCs: nothing Massif does as it starts waits on the disk, the network or Explorer any more, and the pictures of the home screen and the loads run below the window's priority, so that a computer with few cores still draws it. Should a frame ever keep Massif busy for more than five seconds, at the start or later, `startup.log` now says where.

**Exports in each version's own format.** A world exported for Minecraft 1.18.2 or later (1.19, 1.20, 1.21 up to 1.21.11, 26.1, 26.2 and 26.3, now in the list too) is written as that version writes its worlds itself, so the game no longer converts every chunk the first time it loads it: the world opens quicker and nothing can go wrong in a conversion. Massif knows every block and biome of every release since 1.18.2: one the version does not have yet becomes the closest it has (a cherry or pale oak log a birch or dark oak log, a cherry grove a meadow, a pale garden a dark forest), and a block renamed since takes the version's name (short grass is grass before 1.20.3, an iron chain a chain before 1.21.9), where the game would have dropped them or left holes. Objects one block wide, which the export left out, now stand in the world.

**Graphics presets: Massif runs well on modest PCs too.** A new **Settings ▸ Graphics** page offers **Low**, **Medium** and **High**, or **Custom** if you change any one setting yourself, and every change applies at once, without a restart. It sets the size the 3D views are drawn at (Low draws them at two thirds and takes about half the time), edge smoothing, fog, water reflections, the game's textures in the player's view, how much of a huge map the 3D view keeps on the graphics card (a larger map is drawn with a column every few blocks: all of it, coarser, and far faster), the light and clouds of the Terrain viewport (the clouds cost the most there; saved images keep them), the map view's images on the graphics card, and how often a window that is left alone keeps drawing. On its first start Massif picks a preset for your graphics card after drawing a few frames as a trial (Low on OpenGL and older integrated graphics, Medium on recent integrated graphics, High on a graphics card of its own) and never changes one you chose. If the 3D views stay slow while you move them, a quiet note offers the next lighter preset, once.

**Your own keyboard shortcuts.** **Settings ▸ Keyboard** lists every shortcut of Massif in columns (General, Tools, Brushes, Map, 3D view, Player), with a search. Click one and press the new keys; if another action already has them, Massif names it and asks whether to replace it. Start from Massif's keys or WorldPainter's (⌘Y to redo, ⌘ with +, − and 0 to zoom the map), put one action or all of them back, and export or import your keymap to take it to another computer. The menus, macOS's menu bar too, show your keys, and shortcuts wait while you type in a text field, but for those with ⌘ (Ctrl) such as Save. Your keys are kept through updates.

**A big brush held in place stays smooth and shows the land as it is.** With a large brush (a radius of 500, say) held still over the map, squares of the 2D map inside it could stay as the land was before, as if those parts reacted differently: each frame redrew only the parts nearest the middle of the view, and the others waited for as long as the brush was held. Now the parts waiting longest are redrawn first, so all of them keep up, and a frame always draws a little, however slow. The heights the brush writes were always the same on every tile. A held brush was also slow with the 3D view open: the 3D view copied the map and rebuilt the tiles under the brush on every core but two, over and over. It now rebuilds them once the brush is let go, and a frame takes a half to two thirds less of the processor's time (radius 506 on a map of 4,096 blocks a side: Raise 54–59 ms down to 18–30 ms, Smooth 70–72 ms down to 21–28 ms).

**Report a problem in one click.** **Help ▸ Report a Problem…** makes one `.zip` file to send us on Discord when Massif crashes or is slow, instead of digging for logs and screenshots. It holds what happened in your words, Massif's version, your computer and graphics card, the settings that change how Massif draws, the map's size, the last minute of frame times, memory and processor use, and the logs of the last two starts; the map itself only if you tick **Include the map**. You see every file before saving, and can open each one as it will be written: your home folder is written `~` and other accounts' names are left out, and nothing is sent from Massif. **Copy Summary** puts a few lines on the clipboard for your message. For slowness, **Start Recording**, do the slow thing, then **Stop**: the report then also has a timeline of every frame and of what took its time. After a crash, the dialog that offers your map back has **Report the Problem…** too.

**The 3D view shows the real blocks.** The 3D View and 3D Sculpt used to draw every block in one flat colour, so the blocks you painted, Conquest Reforged's purple tiles say, showed as plain squares. In the Terrain look each block now shows its own texture, from Minecraft and from the mods and resource packs read in the Blocks panel: grass, flowers and snow tint the top they grow on, trees show their bark and leaves, overhangs and caves are textured too, and the corners between blocks are shaded as the game's smooth light shades them. Far off, where a block is smaller than a pixel, it blends into the colour of its texture, so the land stays smooth without flicker. It is on in the Medium and High graphics presets; Low keeps the flat colours, and **Settings ▸ Graphics ▸ Game textures in the 3D views** turns it on or off in any preset (it also sets the player's view). Cherry and pale oak leaves are now pink and pale as in the game, where they used to come out green.


**Base trees, a sub-canopy and tree sizes, for forests as the Conquest Reforged team paints them.** A block has one base plant layer and one base tree layer: painting another over it takes its place, so two plants or two species never grow on one block. An object layer can now be a **sub-canopy** layer (Canopy ▸ Sub-canopy in its settings): it is painted beside the base trees instead of in their place, and its objects (hazel, holly, bushes) grow under their canopy, in the air the trees leave, never through a trunk or a crown; the Bushes and Azalea bushes of Packs are sub-canopy layers. The new **Tree sizes** tool (Decor group, and four swatches in the Layers panel) marks where bushes, small, medium or large trees grow: paint the sizes first, then one species over everything, and each spot takes that species' objects of the size marked, a layer's objects being split by height into four sizes. The rest of WorldPainter's layers also come with a `.world` now: caverns, chasms and caves are carved where they were painted, tunnel layers become levels, custom ground cover layers become terrains, and combined layers bring the layers they hold with their terrain and biome.


**Rivers meet the sea naturally, with sandy shallows.** A river dug with the River tool keeps gravel in the middle of its bed, but its shallows are now sand: the edges of the bed and the inside of each bend, where the current is slow, with a strip of beach at the foot of the bank there. At the sea it no longer ends against the coast: its channel goes on under the water, cut into the sea floor and down it, shallower and shallower until it fades into the floor, with sand on its floor and a fan of sand where it ends, the river's biome thinning out into the sea's. Its water meets the sea at its level (where it reached the sea over a beach as high as the water, its last stretch used to stand a block under the sea's surface), and the lakes and rivers it runs into keep their floor and water.


**One Layers panel, with a lock.** The Layers panel now lists every layer of the map by the slot of a block it paints: terrain mixes, ground covers (plants, Frost, Lava), trees and objects, the sub-canopy under the trees, then the tree sizes and the annotations, as the new page Layers of the guide explains. Each row has its eye and a lock: a locked ground cover or tree layer keeps its blocks, so painting another layer of its slot, or the right button, leaves them as they are until you unlock it — paint a new forest around the one you placed by hand without touching it. Its menu opens its settings in a dialog of their own (Settings…), and moves it up or down its section.


**Rivers shaped by the land.** A river dug with the River tool was the same channel everywhere: the same rounded bed, a width growing evenly from source to mouth, banks of one width. Now its shape follows the land: on gentle ground it is a little wider, over a flat bed with rounded sides and patches of clay where the water runs slowly; where the land is steep it is narrower and shallower, cut in a V. Its width wanders a little along its course, as a real river's does, and where it lies deep under the land around it, its banks open out into a valley sloping down to the water (up to 48 blocks wide) instead of the walls of a trench.


**Every block of a mod within reach.** The Blocks panel showed only a mod's whole blocks at first, and sorted many of its blocks under Other: a tester with Regions Unexplored found a couple of leaves and a few terrain blocks out of hundreds. A block whose name says nothing of its family is now sorted by how it is drawn (a mod's flowers and crops with the plants, its fences, doors and signs with the wood), a mod's whole blocks of ground (its grass blocks, dirts, muds, sands, ashes) go with the soils, plants show beside the whole blocks without ticking **All shapes**, and the search looks through every block and shape. With Regions Unexplored, 433 of its 835 blocks show at first instead of 214, and its 25 ground blocks are under Soil, sand and snow instead of none; with Biomes O' Plenty, 215 of 429 instead of 119; with Oh The Biomes We've Gone, 536 of 965 instead of 311. For a block nothing finds, type its id under the search, with its properties if it has any (`mod:block[axis=x]`), and paint it **As terrain** or grow it **As cover**: a block Massif has not read is written as typed and drawn in grey.


**One-block steps read on the 2D map further out.** With **Block steps** on (the default), the map showed each step of a block as a sharp line only close up, where a pixel is a block or less; a little further out it went back to a smooth shading where gentle slopes looked soft and their steps disappeared, as testers found. Where a pixel spans 2 × 2 or 4 × 4 blocks, the hillsides now keep their smooth light and each step draws its line over it, thinner and fainter the further out, as WorldPainter shows them. Turning **Block steps** off still gives the smooth look at every zoom.


**Underground pockets of gravel, clay or a mod's stone, painted with a brush.** The new **Underground pockets** tool (Decor group) lays blobs of other blocks in the rock under the ground, as WorldPainter's layer of that name: a pocket layer is made of blocks of your own, with their weights, and takes its share of the rock where it is painted, in pockets about its size across, between the heights you give it. The pockets stay in the rock: the grass and dirt of the ground over them, caves and water keep their blocks. **New pockets** offers gravel, dirt, clay, andesite, diorite, granite and tuff, or any full block of the game or a mod; the pockets show hatched over the map while the tool is in hand, and they have their own section in the Layers panel, with a lock. Ores grow in pockets of rock (andesite, granite, diorite, tuff) as in the rest of it, and the survival check and the Ores window count the pockets' blocks where the export lays them: a pocket of diamond blocks is caught as riches lying around. A `.world`'s underground pockets now come in as pocket layers of the same blocks, as frequent and as large, between the same heights.


**Rivers that wind like rivers.** The course of a river from the River tool could loop back on itself near its source, where its water had wandered round a shallow hollow before spilling out, and ran in straight lines and stairs along the map's grid where its way had been found from cell to cell. Its loops are now cut straight across (never over higher ground), its runs along the grid are smoothed, and on gentle ground it meanders gently, about half its width to either side over some ten times its width, without climbing out of its valley; the points you drag it through stay where they are, and the course shown before digging is the one dug. On "Continent and islands", a river that took 946 blocks to reach the sea, a hook of 400 blocks round a hollow near its source, now gets there in 483.


**Clearing and combining selections is easy to find.** Right-click the map or press Esc with a selection tool in hand to clear the selection, or press **Clear**, now right under the **New · Add · Subtract · Intersect** buttons of Tool Settings beside **All** and **Invert**. Shift or ⌘ (Ctrl on Windows and Linux) while dragging adds a shape, Alt or the right button takes it out, and the tool's hint and card say so. A click without dragging now really clears the selection in the New mode, where it used to select the block clicked. The keys that add and take out can be changed in Settings ▸ Keyboard.

**The tools' column is as wide in every workspace.** It was a little wider in Layout than in Sculpting and Painting, so the map's edge moved when switching between them. The three now give it the same share of the window, and a layout saved before is changed where its column was left as it came; one you resized by hand stays as it is.

**The map with Block steps is as bright as before.** Shaded block by block, the 2D map came out darker than the smooth shading of 0.6, the more so on hillsides: a step lit by the light was much fainter than a step in shadow was dark. A step of one block is now lit as much as it is shadowed, by the light of the slope it stands for, so the map keeps 0.6's brightness while every step still shows as a sharp line.


**The whole map's rivers, as natural as the River tool's.** Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Rivers dug every river as the same channel, and painted gravel over its banks too, a grey band along both sides of every stream. Its rivers are now shaped as the River tool's: narrower and in a V down steep valleys, a little wider over a flat bed on gentle ground, their width wandering a little, their banks opening out into a valley where they lie deep under the land, and into the sea their channel goes on under the water, fading into the floor. Gravel and sand go only under the water (sand in the shallows and in the channels under the sea); the banks keep their grass.


**Combined layers: several layers in one stroke, as in WorldPainter.** The new **Combined layer** tool (Decor group, and the first section of the Layers panel) paints a forest's terrain, biome, ground cover and trees at once. Its settings name the layer of each slot it paints — terrain, biome, cover, trees, sub-canopy, tree size, underground pockets — and the share of the columns each takes, ferns over 60 % of them say, the same columns every time the brush goes over them. Each layer goes to its slot as its own tool paints it, locks included, so a block still holds one layer of each slot, and one stroke is one step to undo; the right button rubs out what it paints, the terrain put back as Paint terrain's right button does. A `.world`'s combined layers now come in as combined layers to keep painting with, with the layers they hold at their factors.


**Rivers on very large maps.** Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Rivers drew no river at all on a very large map: a river needed half a percent of all the map's land to drain through it, and on a map of 44,544 × 33,536 blocks no valley gathers that much. On such a map a catchment of some 900 blocks a side is now enough (from 200 to 4,000 with the setting), and that map gets its rivers in about 80 seconds; maps of a few thousand blocks get the same rivers as before. Its export also no longer spends time settling water where there is none to see: on that map, whose water level lies under the ground almost everywhere, working out the water as the game would leave it took 27 seconds and now takes 3.


**WorldPainter's River layer comes in.** A WorldPainter map whose rivers were painted with its River layer lost them when opened in Massif: the layer was listed as not imported. It is now dug where it was painted, as WorldPainter's own export digs it: the water two blocks under the ground, the bed four to seven blocks under the water and shallower towards the edges, joining a lake or the sea nearby at its level. Exported, its ground and water match WorldPainter's own export to the block in 78 of 80 columns checked along a river (the other two a block apart). Its bed is Massif's rivers' (gravel, sand in the shallows, clay in patches) with the river biome.


**Clicking the Gradient brush again over the same edge paints the same thing.** A second click used to take the blocks the first one laid (moss, coarse dirt, the first terrain scattered past the edge) for a new boundary and spread the gradient further each time, eating a sand shore and painting the sea floor. The brush now finds the boundary between the gradient's first and last terrains only and paints only those two: its middle terrains are the transition it laid, a terrain it does not paint (a beach, a field) stays as it is, and so does the ground under water. It remembers the boundary it found, so clicking again over the same edge changes nothing, and a soft brush only fills in the rim its first click left half painted.


**The 3D view stays smooth on large maps.** On a large map with much water or many trees, each tile the 3D view drew in blocks cost the graphics card a call of its own, thousands of them a frame, and switching the 3D view between Terrain, Height, Slope, Biome and Relief rebuilt the map while the frames crawled: on a map of 16,384 blocks a side at the High preset, Massif 0.6 drew each frame of a switch in 21 to 29 ms on average, with stalls up to 70 ms, for 9 to 17 seconds. The 3D view now draws all those tiles in a few calls: the same frames take 2.7 to 4 ms (8 to 9 ms for the slowest twentieth), the whole map seen from afar draws in 11 ms instead of 22, and a map rebuilt for another colouring reads each of its tiles once instead of a dozen times, with a sixth less work for the processor. The Medium and Low presets, which keep a column every two blocks on maps that large, were smooth already and stay so.

**The map's sides show its section in 3D.** Seen whole from afar, the sides of a map in the 3D view took the colour of its tops, so a grassy map stood on tall green walls streaked with the colours of the grass above. They now show the land in section, as up close: the top block and the soil under it in a thin band, the rock down to y 0, the deepslate below, in flat colours or with the game's textures; a cliff seen from afar keeps its rock the same way. The small steps of a slope still blend into the grass far off, without stripes.


**WorldPainter layer files (experimental).** A custom layer exported from WorldPainter (Export in its menu, a `.layer` file) no longer has to be made again by hand: **Import WorldPainter layer…**, at the top of the Layers panel, reads several at once, and dropping them on the window does the same. Plant layers become ground covers with the same plants; custom object layers become object layers of their objects, Bo2 trees, schematics and structures read from the file, with their offset, frequency, random turn and density; ground covers become a ground cover of their blocks laid over the land, or a terrain of them where they take the place of the top of the land; underground pockets and combined layers (with the custom terrain written with them) become Massif's. A report says what each file became and what was not carried over: tunnel, floating and custom annotation layers, objects' collision, leaf decay and foundation settings, entities, a ground cover's edges and noise. Your map's own layers are never changed: a layer of the file with the name of one of yours comes in as a layer of its own. Also from `.world` files, old materials known only by their number (as in older custom terrains and ground covers) now come in as their block rather than as stone, and a custom object layer named like a tree of WorldPainter's tree pack keeps its own objects.


**Whole-map lakes and rivers that hold their water**

Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Lakes no longer leaves its lakes a block above their shore with a wall of water around them: each lake fills its hollow exactly to its rim, block by block, in a bowl that deepens away from the shore, sand under its shallows and a sand beach where the shore is flat. Whole map ▸ Rivers no longer raises dams of land across its beds at the steps, leaves sand or gravel on dry banks, or one-block islands in its water; a lake it makes stands at most a block over the water beside it; its narrowest rivers are a quarter of the Width set, and the tributaries thinner than that are left out. The 3D views draw water as the game does: flowing water down each step of a river, its surface sloping, instead of a vertical wall.


**The 2D map shows where the 3D view is**

The small red cross in the map was only the world's origin (x 0, z 0) and did nothing, which looked like a broken marker. When a workspace shows the 3D view beside the map, the map now marks where the 3D view is, a dot in the theme's accent colour with a wedge the way it looks (ringed while walking as the player), following it as it moves; drag the dot to move the 3D view there. The origin stays as a small white plus in a dark outline, readable on any land and in every theme.


**A Massif menu on Windows and Linux**

Settings no longer hides in the View menu on Windows and Linux. A first menu, Massif, holds what the Mac's app menu does: About Massif, Settings… (Ctrl+,), a new Check for Updates… that asks GitHub at once and shows the answer, then Full Screen (F11, new too) and Quit (Ctrl+Q, which asks first when the map has unsaved changes). On a Mac, the app menu stays as it was.


**The map's brushes work again where you sculpted in 3D.** A stroke in 3D Sculpt, Smooth above all, made sculpted cubes of 16 blocks over the whole reach of its brush, most of them holding nothing of their own, and each kept its cube as it was: the ground changed there later by a brush on the map, or flattened over the whole map, did not show, and islands of the old land stood where no brush seemed to do anything. Strokes in 3D now keep only the cubes they change, a brush on the map that moves the ground under sculpted matter takes it along, and a map opened lets go of the cubes that hold nothing, saying how many (on a map smoothed in 3D for minutes, 9,643 of its 11,337).


**A stroke no longer stops Massif when something else changes the map under it.** Smoothing in 3D Sculpt for a while could end on "History::begin was not called": while a stroke was held, something else closed its step to undo (an undo, a selection made with Esc, ⌘A or ⌘D, a task's or the terrain graph's result put in place), and the stroke's next dab had no step to record into. A stroke now notices and records the rest of itself as a step of its own, tasks finishing during a stroke wait for it to end, and an edit with no step open is recorded in a new one rather than stopping the app. When a frame does stop on an error, the stroke it cut short is taken back, in the map and in the copy Massif keeps of it, so that neither holds half a stroke.

**The 3D views say why they show no textures**

Up close at High, the 3D views could turn into flat colours, a square a block, with nothing to say why: Massif had not found Minecraft to read its textures from, or the graphics card could not draw them. Massif now also looks for the game where Prism and the Modrinth App keep it on Windows, macOS and Linux; when it still finds none, or the graphics card fails, the views keep their flat colours and Settings ▸ Graphics says why under Game textures in the 3D views, as does startup.log.


**Rivers that widen where valleys join them**

A river dug with the River tool widened evenly from its source to its mouth, whatever the land around it. It now widens as the land draining into it grows, found the way water runs over the ground around its course: little along a stretch that gathers nothing, over some thirty blocks where a valley joins it, as wide as Flow sets at its mouth. A lake it fills now stands at or under the lowest point of its rim, never a block over it.


**Fly through the ground into caves with Ghost.** 3D Sculpt's Player has a third way to move beside Walking and Flying: **Ghost**, chosen at the bottom right of the view or with G (its key can be changed in Settings ▸ Keyboard), flies through everything, as the game's spectator mode does, to go into caves, under overhangs and along tunnels and sculpt or paint there. With your eyes in the ground the view sees through it, its edges darkened and **In the ground** said in the bar, to the air beyond and the walls and floor of the caves there, and the cursor and the brush work on the surface shown. The flight speed is Ghost's too; G again flies out, from the first air above if you are in the ground.

**3D Sculpt works with the tools of the Tools panel.** Its own Sculpt, Smooth and Paint buttons are gone: it uses the tool chosen in the Tools panel, with its Tool Settings and Brush Settings, exactly as the map does, and its workspace now shows those three panels beside the view. Raise / Lower sculpts in 3D at its own speed, into overhangs and caves; Smooth smooths exactly as on the map (the same heights from the same stroke, the brush's shape, a stamp too, only shaping its falloff), its outline laid on the land over exactly the columns it takes, where it used to mark a different, jagged shape and leave the slopes in steps; Paint terrain paints the columns and the matter sculpted there; the Gradient brush, Paint biome, covers, objects, the other layers and the height tools act on the columns where the cursor points, and the Eyedropper, Flood and Drain where you click. A tool of the map only, a selection shape say, says so at the top of the view, where the buttons then turn and move the view. The top of the view names the tool in hand and the bar along the bottom of the player's view lists what its buttons do. A 3D Sculpt workspace laid out before gets the new panels once, unless you had given it the Tools panel yourself.


**Block palettes: new maps of Conquest Reforged's blocks, or of your own.** A tester asked to generate a world straight away with Conquest Reforged's blocks rather than the game's. The New map settings now have **Blocks**, a palette for the terrains: **Vanilla**, **Conquest Reforged** (its grass blocks, loamy dirt, limestones, sands, gravels, pebbles, snow over icy limestone and glacier ice, several of each mixed in patches as Conquest's own terrain is, from the lists Conquest writes for WorldPainter), or one of your own. The surface the generator lays by height and slope follows it, and so do beaches, river and lake beds, snow and the other natural terrains. **Edit palettes…** makes your own: duplicate one, or make one from the open map, then give each terrain its layers and blocks with their weights, picked from the game's and the mods' blocks or typed by id, and set the rock where caves are carved and ores laid. **Blocks** in the Info panel makes a whole map of another palette at once, in one step to undo, and the map keeps its palette.


**A closed 3D view no longer slows the map down**

On a huge map, closing the 3D view left it building the tiles of the whole map in the background, on nearly every core, for a minute or more: the 2D map stayed slow after it. A 3D view out of sight now stops building at once, and after 20 seconds gives back the memory it holds on the graphics card; opening it again builds what it shows. Its building threads are also fewer on processors with many cores, and on Windows they run below the interface's priority.

**A map opened is always in view.** Opened from the home screen, the recent maps or a backup, a map could show as a black background: framed while the map view had no room yet, a few points high, it came out at 1 %, and a drag at that zoom took the view thousands of blocks away. The map is now framed once its view has room, and framed again when the view grows before you move it. **View ▸ Fit the whole map**, the Home key (in Settings ▸ Keyboard) and the button by the zoom bring the whole map back into view at any time.


**No more giant lakes over whole maps**

Edit ▸ Whole map ▸ Lakes and Rivers could flood a wide hollow of a generated map into a lake hundreds of blocks across. A lake now covers at most a 64th of the map's land (64 blocks a side at least; with Rivers, four times more or less with the Lakes setting): in a wider hollow, its water stands lower, a lake in the bottom of the hollow, still held by its rim. A hollow almost flat all over stays whole.


**Real coasts, lagoons and lakes come out right**

Edit ▸ Relief of a Real Place and New World from a Real Place made low coasts a wide sand plain dotted with square pools, left rectangles and straight seams in the sea and on some capes, and painted all the water as plains. The coastline now follows a smooth line through the elevation data (which swings either side of 0 m along a coast), the beach is a narrow strip, and the sea floor deepens from the shore with no rectangle of the data's sources showing; where fine data sits in rectangles over a coarse fill, as along Sweden's coast, the fill takes the fine data's coast. Lakes the data gives flat are water at their own level. The sea gets ocean biomes (deep where deep, warm or cold by latitude), lakes and rivers river, the sand beach. A tile the server does not send is asked for again, then made from coarser data with no seam, and the status bar and the log say how many.


**Rivers down a slope run in a valley, not down a staircase**

Down a moderate slope, a river dug with the River tool (or Whole map ▸ Rivers) stood in box-like pools from step to step, its banks a staircase of grass ledges on both sides. It now runs down in rapids, a block at a time, its banks sloping down to it as one smooth valley along the whole run. Pools and falls are kept for really steep ground (a grade of some 30 %), fewer and rounder, and the banks ramp down past each fall instead of stepping.


**Flood anywhere, warned first**

Clicked with the Flood tool on a spot that is not in a hollow (a slope, a hilltop, flat ground), Flood refused. It now asks: made to stay a block over the spot, the water would spread wherever the land lies lower, and the question says over how many columns and up to what level, with **Flood anyway** to do it (one step to undo, inside the selection when there is one). **Warn before flooding beyond a hollow**, in Tool Settings and on by default, can be turned off to flood at once.


**Every mod's blocks the same way.** The Blocks panel now finds the instances installed here with any mod that has blocks, not just Conquest Reforged, and lists those not read yet under "Mods with blocks in your Minecraft instances", each with its mods' names and the version it plays; Use reads it in one click. The Blocks menu (Info ▸ World, and the New map settings) lists Vanilla, the palettes of the mods read for this map, and your own: a mod's palette, such as Conquest Reforged's, is offered only once its blocks are read. Mod palettes are data files shipped with Massif: besides Conquest Reforged's, Biomes O' Plenty, Regions Unexplored and Oh The Biomes We've Gone now have one, and the guide says how to write one for any other mod. The Experimental badge beside "Import WorldPainter layer…" stays on one line in a narrow panel.


**Flood raises and lowers water a block at a time**

Clicked on a lake, Flood now raises it by one block, over the shore a block above it, and asks first when a block more would spill over the rim of its hollow. Its right button lowers the lake clicked by one block, leaving the shore it uncovers as the ground was, until the last layer goes, instead of draining the whole lake at once; Shift + right click drains it whole. Held down, either button keeps going at a steady pace, 6 blocks a second by default (**Hold speed** in Tool Settings), up to the rim or down to the bottom, with the 2D map and the 3D views following, and the whole press is one step to undo.


**The world's origin no longer looks like a pointer**

The small white plus at x 0, z 0 on the 2D map was taken for the pointer. It now shows only with the tile and chunk grid, smaller and fainter.


**The 3D view of a huge map shows at once, never black**

Opened on a very large map, the 3D view used to show a large flat black shape until its tiles were built, and took about ten seconds to show the whole map. It now shows all of the map within about two seconds, from what the 2D map has already read, then refines it from near to far; a part not built yet is never drawn black. The note suggesting a lighter graphics preset no longer appears while the tiles are being built, only when the 3D views stay slow; its button applies the preset and its × stops the suggestion for good.


**One clear choice for the water's height, and three water tools that look like what they do**

The Water brush and Flood each take the water's height from one choice in Tool Settings, **Water height**: **Where I start** (the brush fills to the height where each stroke starts; for Flood, **Where I click**: the hollow up to where it would spill), **Sea level**, or **Fixed**, with its level shown only in that mode, and a line under it saying in plain words what will happen. Over the map, a tag by the cursor says the level the tool fills to (**Fills to y 74**) or why the ground stays dry (**Dry here: the ground is at or above y 62.**). The fixed level is the water's level, not a limit: the only limit is **Height limit**, folded apart with its state in its title. Settings from before carry over (From the click on is Where I start, off is Fixed at the same level). The Drain tool is gone: Flood's right click lowers water a block and Shift + right click drains it whole, and a Drain saved in your settings becomes Flood. The Water group is now the Water brush, Flood and River, with new icons for the Water brush (a brush and a drop) and Flood (a hollow filling up).

**Massif's Discord**

Massif now has a community server on Discord. **Help ▸ Join the Discord…** opens it in your browser, to ask a question, show your maps or share ideas, and **Help ▸ Report a Problem…** links to its **#bug-reports** channel, beside GitHub's issues, as the place to send the report.


**Import mask**

Edit ▸ Import mask… paints an image onto the map, as WorldPainter's Import mask: the annotations (each colour of the image becomes the nearest of the 15, or one colour where it is drawn), any layer (ground covers, trees, under the trees, pockets, tree sizes), a terrain, a biome, water or the height (a heightmap with its offset and scale). The image lands at the world's origin or fitted to the map, with a scale and an offset, shown over the map small before importing; a grey is on from a threshold or a strength scattered over the columns, from black to white or the image's own range, inverted or not, black leaving the map as it is; Replace, Add, Max or Min say how it goes with what is painted. Locked layers keep their columns and the import is one step to undo. PNG, TIFF, BMP and JPEG, grey, colour or 16-bit, are read; large images stream through (16,384² in about 4 s). The image can stay on the 2D map as a guide to trace over, at an opacity, never saved nor exported.


**Every panel fits a narrow window, in every language.** In a small window, or with the sidebar dragged narrow, texts and controls ran past the right edge of their panel and were cut off: Info's name and seed fields, the River's bed, the Blocks panel's buttons, the level buttons, a ground cover's plants, the Road's lists, the render settings, and long titles in German, French, Spanish or Portuguese. Panel titles, settings names and lists now shorten with an ellipsis (whole on hover), buttons go to the next line, and the map's name in the top bar no longer runs over the toolbar's buttons.


**Regions out and back, several masks at once**

File ▸ Export Region… writes a part of the map (the selection, the whole map or blocks typed in) as images of 1 pixel a block: a 16-bit heightmap, an image for each terrain and layer found there, and on demand the biomes, the water and the annotations, with a region.txt that says where it lies. Edit ▸ Import Mask… takes several images at once, each with its own target, all in the same place and as one step to undo; given the images of a region, it puts them back where they came from and gives each the target its name says. A heightmap of a part of the map can fade into the land around it over a number of blocks, without a cliff at the seam.


**Flood stops at the top of the world.** Held down on water with no height limit set (and Warn before flooding beyond a hollow off), Flood raised the water a block at a time for as long as the button was held, on past the top of the world where the game can place no block. It now stops there, and a click on water already at the top says so.


**Dialogs fit a small window.** In a window under about 1,200 points wide or 700 high, the Ores window and Settings ▸ Keyboard ran past both sides of the screen, their Done button out of reach, and tall dialogs such as Real terrain lost their title and their buttons past the top and bottom. The Ores window and the keyboard's columns now take the room the window has, the keyboard's buttons go to a second line, an ore band's settings wrap, and a dialog taller than the window scrolls.


**Search fields keep their text inside.** In the Blocks panel and every other search field (Terrain, Biomes, Packs, a ground cover's or a palette's Add a block, Settings ▸ Keyboard, the help, the graph's node search, the ores' biomes), the start of a long text being typed slid under the field's rounded left edge, and the grey hint sat a little high. The magnifier is now drawn inside the field on its own, the text starts after it and is cut there as it scrolls, and the hint is centred top to bottom. Reported by Fenrir.


**Biomes of mods and data packs.** Once a mod is read in the Blocks panel, the Biomes panel lists the biomes the game, its mods and its data packs define (Regions Unexplored's 78, say, and the instance's data packs), grouped under each mod's name with their own colours, and Auto biome's rules offer them for each kind of land; in the 3D view, grass and leaves take each biome's colours. Any biome can be typed by its id (`terralith:moonlight_grove`) for a mod that is not read here. The export writes them by their ids, so the game shows them with the mod installed. A mod's profile can also give a terrain of one of its blocks a biome (Regions Unexplored's peat mud makes a bayou). The Blocks panel shows more of a mod's plants and ground at first: Regions Unexplored's duckweed, clover, leaf litter, ivy, tassels, dusktrap and hyacinths, and its paths and farmland, which were only found under All shapes.


**Fields and buttons read cleanly in narrow panels.** The Blocks panel's search now takes the panel's whole width, with more room after its magnifier, and the block-id field and its two buttons no longer run past the panel. Buttons such as Import WorldPainter layer…, New combined layer, New cover or Add mods… no longer fold their words onto two lines inside their outline: they keep one line, going under the button before or, in the narrowest panel, cut with an ellipsis (the whole name on hover). The text of every field now sits in its middle, top to bottom, where it sat a point and a half high.


**Ridges behind the home screen**

The home screen now shows, by default, ranges of mountains seen from afar in the colours of your theme instead of a picture: six jagged crests over dark land, one in front of the other, grey with sparks of the accent and white-hot near a large glow of the accent low on the right, as of a sun gone down, under a clean dark sky, all made of the same square dots as before. They drift slowly, the nearer faster, grow quieter where the settings are written, and stop when the window is behind another one. In high contrast only the crests are drawn. Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ **Animate the background** keeps them still, as Reduce motion does. Dropping the pictures makes the app about 18 MB smaller.


**The map's status line no longer runs under its zoom buttons.** In a narrow window, the line under the map saying where the pointer is (its height, terrain, water and biome) was drawn under the zoom slider and buttons at its right. It now stops before them, cut with an ellipsis, the whole line on hover.


**3D Sculpt uses the brush of the Brushes panel**

3D Sculpt no longer has a brush menu of its own: it shapes with the brush picked in the Brushes panel, at the size, intensity and rotation of Brush Settings, exactly as the map does, and a brush picked there is 3D Sculpt's at once. The top of the view shows the brush with its size and intensity; a click on it shows the Brushes panel, which the 3D Sculpt workspace now has under the map. A brush larger than 64 blocks of radius still shapes 64 in 3D, as before: the size shows in the accent, and Brush Settings says so under Size while 3D Sculpt is shown.

The brush also faces the way the land faces over its whole area rather than the face of the one block under the cursor: on a slope of one-block steps it no longer turns on its side when the cursor is over a step's riser. Raise / Lower works straight up on gentle slopes, on the same columns as on the map, and along the surface on cliffs and in caves; Paint terrain shows the columns it paints.


**Rivers keep to the way you give them.** A river laid out with the River tool could run far from the points it was dragged through: let go, its way was worked out again and could take another valley than the one shown, up to a hundred blocks off on steep land; between two points it could wander far from the line joining them; and the bed dug missed the points dragged by up to eleven blocks. Now it goes through every point dragged and ends where you clicked, keeps near the line between them, takes the valley shown while dragging, and digs what was shown.


**A real place in the blocks of your choice.** Edit ▸ Relief of a Real Place… and File ▸ New World from a Real Place… now have the Blocks menu of the New map dialog: Vanilla, your own palettes, and those of the mods whose blocks are loaded, such as Conquest Reforged. A new world from a real place is made of the palette chosen. Into an existing map the menu starts on the map's palette; picking another one switches the map's palette along with the relief, and one undo takes both back.

**The 3D View's wheel brings you right down to the land.** Turning the wheel in the 3D View came closer to the point the view turns about, which on a large map is high over the land: the view stopped tens or hundreds of blocks over the ground and could not come nearer. The wheel now flies toward the land under the cursor, down to a few blocks over it whatever the size of the map, slowing as it nears it, and the view then turns about that point; over the sea it stops at the water's surface instead of going under it. Alt + wheel comes closer around the point the view turns about, as the wheel alone did. Reported by Chonky cow cat.


**Flood raises the water you click, whatever the Water height**

A click with Flood on a lake, a river or the sea raises it a block, and holding the button keeps raising it, whatever Water height is chosen: Where I click, Sea level and Fixed now only set the level of a new fill on dry land. Before, with Fixed at y 63, a click on a lake at y 63 did nothing and told you to switch to Where I click, although the height limit was off. The tag by the cursor says what the click will do, "Fill to y 63" or "Raise this water to y 64", and the only stop is a real one: "Height limit y 80 reached" when the limit is on, or the rim of the hollow when the warning is on.


**Every block up close in the 3D views of huge maps.** On a map too large for the graphics card to hold every block, the 3D View and 3D Sculpt drew it with a column every 2, 4 or 8 blocks even up close, untextured blocks several wide where the player sees one. Once the eyes come low over the land, the views now draw every block, with the game's textures, over about 3 km around them, ready a second or so after you stop, and again as you move on; the rest of the map is drawn as before, and the first view of the whole map still comes within two seconds. Reported by Chonky cow cat.


**Even margins in the panels' headers, and messages that stay off the panels**

The commands in a panel's header sit on its middle line and follow the panel's rounded corner, their text lined up with the panel's content; the "…" menu stays inside the panel's corner even when the header is too narrow for everything, what does not fit fading out before it instead of pushing it over the edge. Messages now show over the bottom right of the map, above its footer, instead of over the Levels and Info panels. The names of settings beside sliders and menus (Speed, Size, Edit, Name…) start at the panel's edge like the rest, instead of floating in the middle of their column, and the map's name in Info ends where the other fields end. The tag by the cursor over the map folds a long note and keeps clear of the map's edges.


**Relief of a Real Place and Caves fit a low window.** In a window under about 760 points high, the bottom of the Relief of a Real Place dialog and of the Caves dialog, their Apply, Carve and Cancel buttons included, was below the window, to be scrolled to. The real place's map of tiles and preview now shrink to the room there is, and Caves lays its settings in two columns, so that both dialogs show whole, buttons included, down to a window 640 points high.


**Terrain, World, Render: the sides in the order of the work**

The switcher at the top left now reads Terrain, World, Render, in the order a map is made: its relief generated, then edited, then shown.
