Render, marked Beta, is the side where Massif 2.0 will make path-traced images of your map, with the game's textures under a real sky; until then it says what it will be. Each side still comes back on the workspace it was left on, and the layouts you saved are kept as they were.


**Choose the home screen's background**

Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ **Home background** offers four backgrounds, shown alive in a picture above their few settings: **Ridges** (the mountains under a glow, made of dots, still the default, now in five palettes, with their height, glow and number of ranges), **Waves** (smooth bands of colour that rise from the foot and melt into each other, as at sunset), **Pixel** (the same waves in large square pixels) and **Prism** (crisp columns of colour drawing a crest, a valley, a tide, a slant or a lens, that expand, gather or breathe). Waves and Pixel come in six palettes, among them one that follows your accent colour, and Prism in six of its own; each palette shows its colours beside its name. Waves can be broader or softer and rise from any side. In the light theme they turn to calm pastels, and over Waves, Pixel and Prism the new map's settings sit on a solid surface. They look right without touching anything, keep the words over them legible in the light theme, the dark one and high contrast, cost almost nothing, and stand still with Reduce motion.


**A river never runs into a lake that stands higher than it.** A river let go at a spring with the River tool fills the hollows on its way with lakes; dug wide and deep (a large width, flow, depth or erosion), its water lay several blocks under the land, so it reached a lake from below: the lake stood up to seven blocks over the river that fed it and spilled back into its channel, its water rising downstream. Above a lake it crosses, a river now stands at the lake's level at least. A branch, a river laid out from water already there, never stands over the river it leaves either.

**No more pit where a river runs off the edge of the map.** A river dug with the River tool that ran off the edge of the map took the land past the edge for the bottom of the world: its water dived over its last blocks and its bed was dug into a pit at the edge, down to y 14 for a narrow river on a plain. It now keeps the level of the land at the edge.

**Water stays still in the game along the edges between tiles.** The export works out the water of a map 128 blocks at a time; where a river or a lake crossed the edge between two such tiles, each side was worked out without what the other wrote, and the first block a player changed nearby set the water moving there: flowing water evened out, and sources appeared (up to 9,000 blocks on a plain crossed by a wide river). The tiles are now made to agree along their edges before the world is written.

**Lowering the shore of a lake widens it.** Lowering, flattening or smoothing the land beside a lake or a river under the level of its water left a dry hole beside it, which the game then filled with running water. The water now flows into the land lowered beside it, across everything the stroke lowered.

**WorldPainter's River layer keeps its water in its bed on a slope.** Painted across a hillside, the River layer's water stood over the lower bank and ran out over the land in the game; the bank now rises back to hold it, or the water goes down to what holds it.


**Smooth terrain.** Edit ▸ Smooth terrain… builds the top of the land in partial blocks when the map is exported, following its precise height instead of whole blocks: layers by eighths, slabs, stairs facing each step (inner and outer ones in the corners), vertical slabs at the foot of cliffs and corner pieces, each from the block painted there, of the game or a mod. One switch turns it on for the whole map, and the smoothing follows the terrain: repaint grass as sand and its pieces change with it, with no layer to keep in step by hand. The page sets the pieces each terrain may use; the defaults come from the game and from the mods' profiles, Conquest Reforged's giving its soils layers and its rock the whole range of its models. Pieces in water are waterlogged, and the 3D View shows them. The Smoothing brush turns it on or off in places, or lays a slab of your choice. Asked for by Jack, Fenrir and the builders of Conquest Reforged maps.


**The theme button is gone from the title bar**

The sun and moon button at the right end of the title bar is gone. The theme follows the system unless you choose Light or Dark in Settings ▸ Appearance or in the View menu, and a theme you had chosen with the button is kept. The right end of the bar stays free, for a button to come.


**Flood puts water where you click, and the River tool's points stay where you put them**

Flood's Where I click, now what Flood is set to until you pick another height, puts water wherever you click: in the hollow under the click, or, on a slope or a hilltop, in the hollow the water runs down into, shown by the cursor with a ring before you click; puddles of a few columns are run past, and where the water would run into the sea or off the map, it fills the nearest hollow around the click. With Fixed or Sea level under the land clicked, it fills that hollow instead of saying "Dry here", and says so. Only where no hollow is near does it still ask how far to flood. The River tool adds a point exactly where you click, at the end, and never moves the points already laid: before, a third click moved the end instead of adding a point. A click on the river puts a point between the two that stretch joins, the points are numbered, a click on a handle without dragging leaves it where it is, a right click takes a point away and the others stay, and a quick click on a slow frame is no longer lost. A click on Dig river or Cancel in the bar over the map digs or drops the river instead of going through to the map and adding a point behind it (Build road and Cancel too, and the 3D view's walk bar), and the messages at the map's corner stay above that bar, where they covered Cancel.


**WorldPainter's scripts run in Massif**

File ▸ Run Script… runs a WorldPainter JavaScript script on the open map as it is: its height maps and masks, layers (WorldPainter's own and `.layer` files), terrains and custom `.terrain` files, filters, and worlds made from height maps, saved and exported. The dialog asks for the script's parameters, shows what it prints and the line of an error, has a progress bar and Stop, and the whole run is one step to undo. On the command line, `massif-cli script my.js arguments…` runs one too. Scripts give the map WorldPainter gives, checked column by column against WorldPainter itself, and fast: 600 masks on a 4096 × 4096 map take 8 seconds, where WorldPainter takes 6 minutes. What Massif does not do yet stops the script with "… is not supported yet". A script may only use files in its folder or ones you give it, and has no network. See docs/scripting.md and "Coming from WorldPainter scripts".

**Scripts in Lua, Massif's own API**

Besides WorldPainter's scripts, File ▸ Run Script… and `massif-cli script` run scripts written for Massif itself, in Lua (Luau): the open map is `massif.map`, or open, create, save and export maps; read and write rectangles of columns at once (heights, water, terrains, biomes, layers, annotations); paint masks from images in Massif's own terms with `map:import_mask` (600 masks on a 4096 × 4096 map in under 3 seconds); run Edit ▸ Whole map's passes (erosion, rivers, lakes…) with `map:whole_map`. Lua scripts run in a sandbox: no files but those they may use, no network, no programs. It is the API Massif's plugins will be written with. See docs/scripting.md.


**Glass has its textures again with Minecraft 26.1 and later.** From 26.1 the game writes the texture of glass, stained glass, glass panes and a few other see-through blocks in a new form that Massif did not read: with 26.1 or 26.3 these blocks had no texture and showed grey. They are read again, and marked see-through; older versions of the game read exactly as before.


**The 3D views no longer crash or freeze on large edited maps.** On a map too large for every block, a tile wholly covered by a level or an overhang (none of its columns drawn by the ground's tracer) closed Massif as the 3D view built it ("index out of bounds"); such columns are now drawn as rock at that scale. And the 3D views no longer hold the window still for seconds after long editing: what they copy of the map to build from is prepared away from the window.


**Brush previews stop at the edge of the map**

With the pointer near the edge of the map, the hatching of Auto biome and Auto paint, the brush's strength, the colours of a noise and a selection's marching ants were drawn over the dark void round the map as well. They now stop cleanly at the map's edge, on maps of any shape; only the brush's outline goes on over the void, faintly, so that its whole size still shows.


**Massif in Russian.** **Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ Language** now also offers Русский, and Massif picks it by itself on a Russian system. The whole interface is translated, with the names Minecraft gives its blocks and biomes in Russian, and counts take Russian's own forms (1 блок, 2 блока, 5 блоков). Every panel, dialog and menu fits the smallest window in Russian too. The help and the online guide stay in English for now.


**At home from WorldPainter.** The first start asks "Coming from WorldPainter?". Yes lays Massif out as WorldPainter: a new WorldPainter workspace with the map big in the middle, the tools on the left and Terrain, Layers and Brushes on the right, WorldPainter's keyboard shortcuts (⌥M for Raise Mountain too), and a tour of eight steps, "Where are my WorldPainter tools?", that lights up where your .world files, height brushes, terrains, layers, water, selections and export are, then what Massif adds. The workspace is the last tab of the World side for everyone, the tour is in the Help menu, and each tool's card says what WorldPainter calls it. docs/coming-from-worldpainter.md and the help map every WorldPainter feature to its place in Massif.

**Render (Beta): the map path-traced, and saved as images**

The Render side now draws the open map path-traced on the graphics card: sunlight and skylight bounce off the land, shadows are soft, water mirrors the sky and shows the floor of the shallows, and glowing blocks (glowstone, lanterns, torches, lava…) light what is around them, with the game's textures and models of slabs, stairs, fences, plants and the rest. The map is built as an export would write it, nearest the view first, and the image grows clean while the view stays still. A look to start from (Clear noon, Golden hour, Foggy morning, Night…), the time of day and the season put the sun; haze, fog with shafts of light, clouds and a sea around the map set the air; a lens gives a depth of field (Shift-click to focus). **Save image…** draws the view at its own size, in HD, 4K or 8K, to the samples a pixel asked for, with its progress and Cancel, and writes a PNG.

**Each 3D View shows its own mode.** Several 3D View areas no longer all follow one another: each has its own mode (Terrain, Height, Slope, Biome or Relief), its own water switch and its own camera, so one view can show the land in Terrain while another shows its slopes and a third its biomes. Each area is remembered with the layout and opens again as it was left, a duplicated workspace keeps them, and a new 3D View opens in Terrain, looking where the first one does.


**A tidy list of your instances' mods**

The Blocks panel's **Mods with blocks in your Minecraft instances** shows each instance on one row, with its loader, the version of the game it plays, how many mods with blocks it has and **Use**, instead of every mod's file name in one long paragraph. Click a row to unfold its mods, one a line, by the names they give themselves (from `mods.toml`, `fabric.mod.json` or the `mcmod.info` of 1.12.2 mods), or their file names without versions and loader tags, with their ids and how many blocks they have; hover one for its jar's file name. A search finds instances and mods by name, id or file, and a modpack of hundreds of mods stays quick to scroll.


**The 2D map no longer shows black squares zoomed out, and shows the pointer**

Zoomed out on a large map, a square or two of the map could stay black until you zoomed in: a part of the map drawn while the tiles it needed were being dropped from memory was drawn with holes, and kept so. It is now always drawn whole, and a part not drawn yet shows the plain background rather than black. The pointer over the 2D map is now the crosshair you chose in Settings ▸ Appearance (dot, cross, circle or Minecraft's plus), white in a dark edge that reads on dark forest as on light sand, stronger in high contrast, in place of the system's thin black crosshair that was lost on dark land; with None, the system's crosshair stays.


**Maps taller than Minecraft's own height keep it in 26.1, 26.2 and 26.3**

A map exported for Minecraft 26.1 or later with build limits past Y -64 to 320 opened cut at 319, as if its height data pack were not there: the game refused the pack, whose overworld lacked a setting 26.1 made required, and offered to open the world without it. The pack now holds each version's own overworld with the map's limits (1.21.11's sky, fog, music and beds kept too), and Minecraft 26.3, 26.2, 26.1.2, 1.21.11 and 1.21.8 load it: blocks stand up to the map's top.


**Floating panels, and the Render side in panels with a timeline**

Any panel can float: **Float** in an area's **…** menu takes it out of the layout into a window of its own over the window, moved by its title and sized by its corner; **Dock back** puts it back, or drag its title with Shift onto an area to dock it there. Floating panels are kept with their workspace. The Render side (Beta) is now made of panels and workspaces like the other sides: **Render Viewport**, **Sun and Sky**, **Camera**, **Render Output** and **Timeline**, in the workspaces **Still** and **Animation**, each area swappable, splittable and floatable, and in a **Render** section of every area's chooser. The **Timeline** keeps keyframes of the camera and the hour, saved with the map: scrub it and the view follows a smooth path between them, or play it.


**Exports onto a USB drive from a Mac open as made**

On a drive formatted for Windows (exFAT or FAT, as most USB drives and SD cards come), macOS writes a hidden "._" file beside every file it writes. Minecraft read the one beside the height data pack's overworld as a part of the pack, failed on it, and opened the world without the pack, cut at its own height. The export now removes those files from the world it writes, and from the data packs it copies in: a world exported onto such a drive opens with its height.


**Ground covers show on the map as thick as they grow, at an opacity of their own.** Zoomed in, a cover at 100 % density took the colour of its plants, the green of grass over grass, and seemed gone, while at 0 % it stood as a solid colour. Its colour now shows in full wherever something grows and lighter where the ground stays bare, so the denser a cover, the more it shows, close up and from afar. Each cover has an **Opacity** beside its colour in its settings (50 % as before): how strongly that colour shows over the ground. The 3D view still shows every plant in its own colour.


**Shapes sculpted in 3D stay when the map's brushes move the land around them.** An overhang, an arch or a cave built in 3D Sculpt went at the lightest click of Raise, Lower or Smooth beside it on the map, and under Smooth in 3D Sculpt, which smooths as the map does. What was sculpted now keeps its shape and rides on the ground under it: it rises or sinks by the whole blocks the land moves there, and the land the brush moved shows all around it. Each stroke is still one step to undo.


**Reference images to trace over**

Pictures can be laid over or under the 2D map to trace over, as WorldPainter's overlay (Edit ▸ Add Reference Image…, or drop a picture (PNG, JPEG, WebP, BMP, TIFF or GIF) on the map). Each is moved, scaled and turned with handles on the map or typed in (its middle, blocks a pixel, rotation), faded, shown or hidden, locked, and set over the map or under it, the map then faded over it. There can be several; they are saved with the map, found again beside it when moved with it, and never exported. A large picture stays smooth at any zoom: it is kept on the graphics card with mipmaps.


**Diorama (Beta): the map from above, as the game shows it**

A new view, **Diorama**, in the **View** section of every area's chooser, shows the map from straight above block by block with the game's textures: the trees, plants, houses and other objects an export would place, the water over the shallows, and relief light and shadows so slopes, cliffs and valleys read. Drag to pan, scroll to zoom down to the blocks, **R** to turn the view, **Space** to recentre; **C** shows the caves under a height moved with **Page Up** and **Page Down**. It sits beside the 2D map, floats, and follows your edits as you paint.


**Import mask: placing the image is precise**

In Edit ▸ Import mask, the Offset sliders no longer jump tens of thousands of blocks at the slightest move: they span the map, from where the image just touches one edge to where it touches the other, a block a step, and any value typed in is kept exactly. Scale spreads in ratios around the scale that fits the map and a block a pixel, and keeps the image's middle where it is. The image can be dragged on the small map with the mouse, and nudged with the arrow keys, a block a press or 16 with Shift. The Offset row is named in full.


**Fixes from the fifth beta's reports**

New mix in the Layers panel makes a mix at once, listed and chosen, its name ready to change. Alt + click picks what is under the cursor, as WorldPainter's eyedropper does: the terrain, or the biome, ground cover or tree layer of the tool in hand, on the map and in the 3D view (Alt with the left button no longer does the tool's inverse: the right button does). In a layer's settings window, Base and Sub-canopy answer the click again while Tool Settings shows the same layer. The right button of a tree layer, a ground cover or a pocket layer rubs out that layer alone, no longer every one of its kind under the brush. On Windows, the game's jar is looked for on every drive and beside the mods chosen (a CurseForge instance on D: or E:), so that Add mods… and Instance… read their blocks. Picking Paint biome shows the map's biomes and Paint terrain its terrains, the view coming back after (Settings ▸ Appearance). Test Export… asks which part of the map to try: the selection, around the view, or blocks typed in.


**Floating panels in windows of their own**

**Float** in an area's **…** menu now opens the panel in a real window of your system: move it anywhere, onto another screen, and size it as any window; the map, the 3D View, the Render Viewport and every other panel work there as in the layout. **Dock back** in its **…** menu puts it back, and so does closing its window. Floating panels are kept with their workspace and open where you left them, on a screen there is if theirs was unplugged.


**Import mask keeps the image as a reference image**

Import mask now leaves the imported picture on the 2D map as a reference image, exactly where it landed, so you can see the source under what it painted. It is on by default, at the opacity you set, and can be turned off with "Keep the image as a reference image". It is kept with the map like any reference image, never exported, and the map's Reference images button shows, fades, moves or removes it. It replaces the guide that was shown only until the map was closed.


**The Render side is as bright on screen as the images it saves**

The Render Viewport showed its image much darker than the PNG that **Save image…** writes from the same camera: the sea nearly black, the land dull. It now shows the same colours as the saved image.


**A flood never stops halfway.** Flood changes up to 67,108,864 columns (a square of some 8,000 blocks a side), and it used to stop wherever it was once it reached them: on a large map, a flood that ran out over low land or the sea, a held raise past the rim of a lake, or a Shift + right click on a sea that large left the water it had laid standing cut off where it stopped, a box of water with sheer walls over the land and the sea. Now a flood, a raise, a lowering or a drain that would change more than that changes nothing, and the message says why.


**A WorldPainter world keeps its terrains and layers apart, with forests as dense as WorldPainter's, and is as quick right after its import as once reopened.** Custom ground covers came in baked into the terrains, a new terrain for every cover over every terrain ("Water Block on Overgrown Small Stones"), thousands on a large map. They now come in as ground covers of their blocks, as high as they are thick, painted where they were, over the map's own terrains. Tree and object layers stood far fewer trees than WorldPainter's export, a dense forest turning into open woodland: the import now plays WorldPainter's placement with the trees' own shapes and gives each layer the spacing and density that stand as many, at every strength painted, and overlapping tree layers all stand mixed rather than the strongest alone. A large world with ground covers or tunnels kept gigabytes of its map unpacked in memory after the import, and was slow until saved and reopened; it is now stored as a reopened map is.


**The 3D View no longer cuts pits in a deep sea.** Where the ocean floor of a map lies at the bottom of the world, at y -64, the part of the 3D View drawn block by block around the eyes showed a pit in the sea: no water over those columns, and sheer walls of water down to the floor of the sea around them. The rest of the map, drawn coarser, showed the sea whole, and the exported world was right. These columns hold their water in the 3D View again, over the floor of the world.


**Import mask: the mask window**

Import mask opens as a window of its own where there is room: the map large with the image over it, which you drag, zoom and pan. See the image over the map at the opacity you choose, the mask alone, what the map has now (its biomes, terrains, layer, water or heights), what the import will make of it, the two side by side with a line to drag, or only what changes, with how many columns change. A legend says what each grey or colour paints, and a histogram with black point, white point, midtones and blur adjusts the mask itself before it is imported. Import is still one step to undo; Smaller goes back to the dialog.


**Reference images stay out of the way of the tools**

A reference image no longer moves under a brush: clicks and strokes over it go to the tool in hand, as on the bare map. Its handles show only with the Pan tool, or after Edit placement in its menu, until Done or Esc.


**Biome colours of Minecraft 26.1 and later**

With the game's 26.1 or later read, swamps, badlands, warm oceans and the other biomes that name their own grass, leaf or water colours have them again in the 3D views and on the Biome map, rather than the colours of plains.

## New in 0.6.0

**Massif in French and German.** The whole interface (menus, panels, tools and their cards, tooltips, dialogs, the home screen, Settings and the macOS menu bar) is now also in French and in German, in the words Minecraft and WorldPainter players use. Massif follows the system's language by default; **Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ Language** picks another, and the change applies at once, without a restart. A text not yet translated shows in English rather than in pieces, and the help and the online guide stay in English for now. Names that belong to your map (layers, levels, workspaces you renamed) stay as you wrote them.

**Share packs with other Massif users.** **File ▸ Export Pack…** makes one `.massifpack` file of the map's layers: pick its object layers (with their trees and other objects), ground covers and terrain mixes, give it a name, your name as its author, a description and a picture (one is drawn from what it holds, or choose your own). Others add it to their packs with **File ▸ Import Pack…**, the **Import…** button of the Packs panel, by dropping the file on the window, or by opening it from the Finder or Explorer. The packs others made show at the top of the Packs panel, each with its picture and its author, and paint like Massif's own; their menu saves a copy to pass on, or removes them. If you already have a pack of that name, Massif asks whether to replace it or keep both under another name. A pack holds only blocks and settings, never anything that runs: Massif checks all of it before adding it, refuses files that are damaged, too large or not packs, and keeps its own copy of each in its folder.

**Numbers you type stay as you type them.** In the new map's size, its depth and the other number boxes, what you type is left alone until you press Enter, Tab or click elsewhere: no completion, no jump to the least or the most while you type. Only then does it become the nearest value allowed: a map side the nearest multiple of 128 blocks (1000 becomes 1024, 5000 becomes 4992), and a small note under the box says what it became and why. Enter in a number box only ends the typing; it no longer also creates the map.

**Dot-matrix loaders.** What shows that Massif is working is now a small grid of dots lighting in a pattern, in your accent colour, instead of a turning circle: on the home screen's previews, the map check, the terrain graph, the brushes and blocks being read, and the tasks in the background. **Settings ▸ Appearance ▸ Loader** offers eight patterns (Orbit, Ripple, Scan, Rain, Bars, Spiral, Sweep, Twinkle), each moving in its own tile so you can see it before you choose. With Reduce motion on, they hold still.

**Massif tells you when a new version is out.** Once a day at most, Massif asks GitHub which version is the latest, in the background and without slowing its start, and sends nothing about you or your maps. When a newer one is out, a small pill at the right of the top bar, and a line above Settings on the home screen, say so; a click shows what is new since your version, and **Open the release page** opens it in your browser to download it. Massif never downloads or installs anything itself. **Skip this version** stops telling of that one, and **Settings ▸ Updates** turns the check off. Offline, it says nothing.

**Selections: tools that act only where you want.** A new **Select** row in the Tools panel marks the part of the map the tools change: drag a **rectangle** or an **ellipse**, draw around an area with the **lasso**, or paint it with the **selection brush**. Shift adds to the selection, Alt takes out of it, both keep what the two hold; a click deselects. **Select by** picks a terrain, a band of heights or the slopes steeper or gentler than an angle over the whole map. **Feather** softens the edge over up to 64 blocks, and **Edit ▸ Select All, Deselect, Invert Selection** (⌘A, ⌘D, ⇧⌘I) do what they say. Once something is selected, every brush, the flood fill, Auto biome and Auto paint, noise painting and **Edit ▸ Whole map** act only inside it, fading along a feathered edge; nothing outside changes. The map outlines it with marching ants (still with Reduce motion). Every change of the selection is a step to undo, it is saved with the map (older versions open the file without it), and **Export** can write **Only the selection**, to try a part of a large map in the game.

**Caves, ravines and caverns.** **Edit ▸ Caves…** carves caves into the rock of the whole map, or of the selection: winding tunnels that branch, with now and then a wide chamber where pillars of rock stand, as in Minecraft; ravines, long, deep and narrow, some cut open to the sky; and large caverns, which can hold a lake of water or lava up to a height you choose. You set how many there are, how large, the heights they keep to (they keep a roof under the ground unless they open to the surface) and how many open to the surface; the same seed always carves the same caves. They are carved in the background as one step to undo, show in the 3D view and in 3D Sculpt, where you can dig them further or fill them, and are exported as real air, water and lava. A map of 8,192 blocks a side gets its caves in about half a second.

**Roads, graded into the land.** A new **Road** tool, among the sculpting tools, lays a road through points clicked on the map: a smooth curve through them that you edit before building it (drag a point to move it, drag the road to add one, right-click or Delete to take one off). **Build road** (or Enter) cuts through the hills and fills the hollows so that the road never climbs steeper than its **Steepest slope**, keeps it level across its **Width**, eases its **Banks** back into the land, and paves it with a trodden path, gravel, cobblestone, stone bricks, any terrain or the Paint tool's noise, clearing the plants and trees off it. Over water it crosses on a bridge, a deck of planks or stone a block over the water, with the water left under it; or, bridges off, it is built up out of the water. It keeps to the selection, the brush filters choose where it is paved, and it is one step to undo.

**Maps of real places.** **File ▸ New World from a Real Place…** (and **From a real place** on the home screen) makes a world of the relief of any place on the Earth, ocean floors included; **Edit ▸ Relief of a Real Place…** puts one into your map, into the selection or over the whole map, as one step to undo. Search the place by name, type its coordinates or its bounds, or drag a small map of the Earth's relief; choose how many blocks a metre, how much taller the relief stands, where the sea is, and whether mountains too tall for the world are squeezed into it or cut off. A picture shows the ground it makes before you apply it. The heights come from the free Terrain Tiles on Amazon's open data, about 30 m apart, downloaded in the background and kept on disk, so a place seen once works offline; a GeoTIFF, a 16-bit PNG or a raw file you downloaded works too. The sea fills what lies under its level, and the automatic paint paints the ground.

**Autosave: a crash no longer loses your work.** While the map has changes not saved, Massif now keeps a copy of it every few minutes, in a folder of its own (never over your file). Should Massif close without saving them, from a crash, a forced quit or a power cut, it offers the next time it starts to restore the copy: the map's name and when the copy was taken, then **Restore** or **Discard**. Saving the map, or closing it, removes its copy, and at most five are kept. The copy is written in the background and the map stays smooth while it is, even a map of 44,544 × 33,536 blocks. **Settings ▸ Autosave** turns it off or sets how often: every 1, 2, 5 (the default), 10 or 15 minutes.

**Save points: named versions of a map.** **File ▸ Save Point…** keeps the map as it is now under a name, such as "before the rivers" or "version 2". The new **Versions** panel lists them with a small picture and their date: **Restore** puts the map back as it was then, as one step to undo; **Compare** draws over the 2D map where the land is higher or lower than then, in the accent colour, and where it was painted differently, in grey, and counts the columns; a point's **…** menu opens it as a new map, as a copy to change or read-only to look at, renames it or deletes it. The points are kept in the map's own file, so they travel with it, and autosave keeps them too. They share every tile they have in common with the map and with each other, so a point costs only what changed since it was made: on a map of 8,192 blocks a side (50 MB), thirty points made between changes here and there added 4 MB, and saving took no longer. Older versions of Massif open such a file as the map alone (saving it from them drops the points).

**A huge map's 2D view: quicker to draw, a third of the memory.** Opening or zooming out on a very large map, the map view now draws the whole of it in less than half the time and work: a map of 44,544 × 33,536 blocks (91,176 tiles) is drawn whole in 1.6 seconds instead of 4.3, with 14 instead of 31 seconds of processor time. What the view keeps of the map to draw it from now takes 137 MB instead of about 450 on that map, and the Developer panel and Settings ▸ Memory count it as it is (they showed 160 MB), with the images on the graphics card beside it. The map looks the same; zoomed far out, a pixel may show a column a few blocks from the one it showed.

## New in 0.5.2

**Massif starts on slow computers.** On some Windows computers (an AMD Radeon RX 6400, for one) Massif 0.5.1 never showed its window, whatever graphics API it tried: it waited, before drawing its first picture, for the WorldPainter brushes and the game's textures to finish loading, which can take minutes on a slow computer with many brushes. It then blamed the graphics driver and set Vulkan, DirectX 12 and OpenGL aside one after the other. The home screen now comes at once: its picture, the new map's preview and the dates of the recent maps follow a moment later, and the loads no longer hold up the window. Massif sets a graphics API aside only when the graphics driver itself is stuck, and says so; the APIs 0.5.1 set aside by mistake are tried again on the next start. `startup.log` names the part of the window being laid out, should a start still be slow.

**Packs: trees, plants and mixes ready to paint.** As in WorldPainter Modernised, a **Packs** tab beside the Layers panel's list holds the sixteen kinds of trees of the tree pack (tall and slender spruces, firs, larches, giant redwoods, big and pale oaks, birches, cherries, acacias, willows, rainforest giants, palms, dead trees, bushes and azaleas, eight of each), twenty-two presets of flowers, plants and water plants, and thirty-nine mixes of blocks for grass, soil, stone, sand, snow and volcanic rock, with cliff strata laid in horizontal beds. A click adds one to the map and picks it to paint; a search finds one by name. Exports for older versions of the game turn the newer woods into the closest older ones, their leaves still persistent.

**A Layers panel.** WorldPainter's custom layers have been in Massif as ground covers (plants, flowers, any blocks), object layers (trees and rocks from schematics) and terrain mixes (noise painting), but their lists were tucked inside the settings of their tools. The new **Layers** panel, under Terrain, lists them all: click one to paint with it, double-click to rename it, click its eye to hide it on the map and in the 3D view (the export still writes it), right-click to duplicate or remove it, and add new ones from its sections. Layouts saved by earlier versions get the panel under their Terrain panel.

**The menus only in the Mac's menu bar.** On a Mac, File, Edit, View and Help are now only in the menu bar at the top of the screen, where 0.5.1 put them: the window's top bar no longer shows them a second time, and keeps its buttons (new, open, save, export, undo, redo and the tools). On Windows and Linux the menus stay in the window.

**Quitting from the Dock asks first.** On a Mac, **Quit** in Massif's menu in the Dock, Q in the app switcher (⌘Tab), and a logout, a restart or a shut-down no longer drop the changes to the map that are not saved: Massif comes to the front and asks first, as **Quit Massif** (⌘Q) does. A logout, a restart or a shut-down waits for the answer: Save or Don't Save, and it goes on once Massif has quit; Cancel, and it stops there. With nothing to save, Massif quits at once, as before.

**A faster export.** Exporting a map to a Minecraft world takes about a quarter less work: a map of 2,116 tiles that took 35 seconds of processor time now takes 25, and a little over 3 seconds instead of nearly 5 on a ten-core Mac. The world written is the same, byte for byte.

**Faster WorldPainter imports and map tiles.** Importing a `.world` takes less than half as long as before (a map of 5,888 blocks a side: 0.33 s instead of 0.88 s), and unpacking the map's tiles, which painting, drawing the map, the picture saved in the file and the export all do, a quarter less. Imported maps and saved files are exactly the same as before.

**A huge map's 3D view built twice as fast again.** On a very large map (tens of thousands of tiles), the 3D view takes half the work it took in 0.5.1 to build, and less than 0.5.0 did: a map of 44,544 × 33,536 blocks went from about 340 to 180 seconds of processor time, under a minute on a ten-core Mac, so the view gets sharp sooner and the rest of the app stays smooth while it builds. The 3D views no longer make their own look pay for the player's Minecraft look either, which weighed on some graphics cards (AMD among them) even when the player's view was off.

**Quicker brushes on large strokes.** Smooth takes about 30 % less work a dab with a large brush, and brushes limited by slope, by hollows and bumps, or by height take 55 %, 20 % and 10 % less; Raise, Lower and the paint brushes a little less too. What they write is exactly the same as before.

**Flatten one way or both, as in WorldPainter.** Flatten's settings now choose which way it moves the land: **Both ways** as before, **Only raise** to fill hollows up to the height and leave the hills, or **Only lower** to cut the hills down and leave the hollows. **Apply theme** repaints what it flattens with the terrain its new height calls for, sand by the sea, grass, rock and snow higher up.

## New in 0.5.1

**The player's view looks like Minecraft with Axiom.** With **Player** on in 3D Sculpt, the view shows the game's own blocks with their textures (read from the Minecraft installed on the computer), lit as the game lights them, corners shaded as its smooth lighting does, under its blue sky with the square sun, its clouds and its fog, deep water darker toward the floor. The blocks the brush takes are marked in Axiom's lavender and the block under the cursor is outlined. The cursor free, it works as Axiom's editor: left drag looks around, the right button uses the tool under the cursor (Alt: its inverse), the middle one picks the block for Paint, Ctrl turns about a point or moves the view, Ctrl + middle sizes the brush, and the wheel sets the flight speed, also shown in the bar along the bottom with what each button and key does. A click takes the mouse as in the game: the right button builds, the left one breaks. The keys are the game's: Shift sneaks and goes down, Ctrl sprints.

**Height limits you can read.** Brush Settings draws the map from the side, cut from west to east through its highest point, with the sea in blue and the heights on a scale beside it. The land at the heights the brush acts on is in the accent, only between the limits' lines, and each limit is a line across it with its height, dragged up or down (Shift: finely). The picture keeps to the heights of the map, so a limit beyond them waits at its edge instead of squeezing the land into a corner, and the picture and its settings make one group.

**File, Edit, View and Help in the Mac's menu bar.** On a Mac, Massif's menus are now in the menu bar at the top of the screen too, as in every Mac app: the same items as the window's menus, with their shortcuts, greyed out when they cannot be used, and kept in step with them. **About Massif**, **Settings…** (⌘,) and **Quit Massif** (⌘Q) are in the **Massif** menu, where Mac apps keep them, and Help has the system's search of the menus. ⌘Q now asks first when the map has changes that are not saved, as File ▸ Quit does, instead of quitting at once. The keys work as before, in the map and in text fields alike; the window's menus show the shortcuts of their items too.

**Fixed.** The terrain generator's viewport no longer turns the land black: looked at from high above, the mist over it came out as 0 × ∞, which the graphics card paints black. A number typed in (the size of a new map, a height, an ore band) counts once it is done, with Enter or by leaving it: typing 1024 no longer stopped at 1, jumped to the least value allowed, and grew from there into a map of tens of thousands of blocks. The menus of the top bar (File, Edit, View, Help) take a click over a hit as roomy as a system menu bar's, not just over their word.

**Ores: taken out with a key, kept to biomes.** In Edit ▸ Ores, Delete (Backspace on a Mac) takes the ore picked out of the map's ores, as the new **Remove** does, and ⌘Z (Ctrl+Z) puts it back; the **+** at the end of the ores adds back one taken out, as it was. The details under the cut are the picked ore's, its colour down their side: the band picked is ringed in the accent as its candle is, the band whose candle the pointer is over is lit, and pointing at a band there lights its candle. An ore can now be laid **only in** some biomes, or in every biome **except** some, ticked on and off in a menu with a search, as Brush Settings picks what a brush acts on: the export, the cut and the amounts follow, and a funnel marks the ore in the strip. Maps saved before keep their ores, and an export without a biome choice is the same as before.

**No more rows missing after a conversion.** Convert to voxels writes the terrain into the map it was started on. One that ended after another map was opened (a new one, say) used to put its tiles into that map, and the two never matched: black rows of missing land were left between them. It now stops and says so, and one started in another dimension waits until that dimension is shown again. Auto paint, Auto biome, Noise paint and the graph's filters over the whole map behave the same way. Saving no longer hands its file to a map opened before the save ended, so the next save of that map can't overwrite the first one.

**The 3D views with OpenGL.** On a graphics card that only OpenGL drives (an Intel HD Graphics 4600, for one), opening a 3D view, a template or a height map stopped Massif with "Downlevel flags VIEW_FORMATS are required". The 3D views, 3D Sculpt and the terrain generator's viewport now draw there, the same images as elsewhere, and saving the viewport's image no longer gives up while a slow card draws it.

**A start that gets past a stuck graphics driver.** On some Windows computers (an AMD Radeon card with Vulkan, for one) Massif stayed in the background with no window: the driver never finished its first picture. The window is now shown before that first picture, which some drivers need. If a start still stays stuck, Massif notices after 12 seconds, offers to start again right away with DirectX 12 (then OpenGL), and keeps to it on that computer; a start that died without a word is noticed by the next one. `startup.log` follows the first pictures step by step, writes down a crash with the file it came from, and says which graphics API was asked for; `WGPU_BACKEND` is read in quotes too. See *If Massif does not start* in the guide.

## New in 0.5.0

**Ores, as Minecraft lays them.** The export now lays ores in the rock — Minecraft adds none to the map's finished chunks — following the game's own veins and heights since 1.18, or those of older versions. **Edit ▸ Ores** shows the map cut through with the ores exactly where they will be and a candle for each band of each ore: drag its ends, its body or its side to move the heights where veins start, where they are the most common and how large they are; beside it, the ore expected at each height in blocks, on a log scale or as a share of the ground. Saved with the map; the export can leave them out.

**Survival check.** **Edit ▸ Analyse the map** counts every block of the map as the export writes it and reads it as a survival player would: in red what breaks survival (diamond blocks or ores lying around, bedrock above the floor, holes into the void, no wood), in amber what is missing (ores, with a way to Edit ▸ Ores; lava for a Nether portal, grass for animals, trees near the spawn), the way from wood to the Nether, what holds up, and how to fix it. Tabs for the relief (heights, steps a player walks, climbs or falls from, water), the blocks and ores, and the biomes; a spot shown on the map in a click; the report copied as Markdown. A few seconds for a map of 5,888 blocks a side, the ores counted where the export lays them.

**A truer terrain viewport.** Cliffs are rock — lumps, grain and beds drawn in the world's own space — instead of faceted, stretched stripes; each point sees as much of the sky as the relief around it leaves it; haze and a low mist give depth at any map size; forests show their crowns and grass its drier patches. While the view moves it is drawn at half the size, so it moves as smoothly as before. The karst towers (and the floating mountains' towers) have sheer fluted walls, rounded shoulders and broad green tops, where they used to end in a spire.

**Choosing what an area shows.** The icon before an area's title opens every editor on one page, in columns: the World side's views, tools and paint, then the Terrain side's generator. The line under them says what the one under the pointer is for, and whether another area shows it already. An empty area holds the same page.

**Fixed.** The height limits of the brush options are in whole blocks, as the game has the land: a column at 63.2 is at 63 (maps from WorldPainter keep fractions of blocks), and the height tools stop on a sharp limit — flattening toward 63.8 the land at or below 63 brings it to 63, no longer 63.1. A turned square or image brush acts on all of its shape, its corners too. The strength drawn under the brush is lighter, keeps to the outline block by block close up, no longer draws a diamond inside square brushes, and can be switched off (Brush Settings ▸ Strength on the map). The line under the map gives the height in whole blocks and the biome under the pointer.

**Height limits, redrawn.** Brush Settings shows the heights of the map itself, as bars from its lowest to its highest land with the sea marked, under the band the brush acts in: drag its ends, or set them in the fields below, between or outside them; it says how much of the map the band covers.

**Split from any corner.** Every corner of an area splits it when dragged into it, not only the top right one: the new area opens on that corner's side, and while dragging, the line of the split and the side it opens on show.

**A start that says what goes wrong.** Massif writes down every step of its start in `startup.log` (in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Massif` on Windows, `~/Library/Logs/Massif` on macOS), with any error, the one before kept beside it, and nothing sent anywhere. When it cannot start or stops on an error, a message says so instead of the process staying in the background with no window; on Windows the window is shown after 3 seconds even when the graphics card is slow to draw its first picture. See *If Massif does not start* in the guide.

**A big map stays smooth.** The 3D view builds a whole map away from the frames, on threads of its own, and puts what it built on the graphics card a little at a time: on a map of 44,544 × 33,536 blocks, a frame went from 29 ms of work to 11 ms while it builds.

## New in 0.4.1

**The whole map at once.** **Edit ▸ Whole map** runs the terrain graph's filters over the whole map: erosion, thermal erosion, rivers (their beds in gravel), lakes, smoothing, sharpening, terraces, strata, and scaling the relief around the sea. Each opens with its settings and the map before and after, runs in the background with its progress, and is one step to undo; the map's paint, its levels and what was sculpted in 3D stay.

**Smoother.** The map glides on when a drag is let go, the zoom glides, and the views no longer stall while the map's images and the 3D tiles are made: on a map of 5,888 blocks, zooming went from 32 ms of work a frame to 6. The 3D view keeps going a little after a turn, flies softly, and draws itself smaller while it moves, sharp again when it stops.

**Faster.** Exporting a map takes about a fifth less work and writes the same files byte for byte; 3D sculpting with a large brush, and rebuilding the 3D view where it was sculpted, take less time; erosion in the terrain generator and in Edit ▸ Whole map takes about a quarter less work and makes the same terrain to the bit.

**Typefaces.** Settings ▸ Typeface sets the interface in the system's own typeface or in Inter, Geist, IBM Plex Sans or Manrope, built in, each shown in itself.

**Developer mode.** Settings ▸ Developer adds a Developer panel to every area's menu: frames a second, the time of each frame, the memory and the processor, in live charts, with what Massif keeps and why it draws again.

**Ten scenes behind the home screen**, and in the light theme each at dawn. The new map's preview stands beside its settings, as tall as they are, and what is written over the picture reads over any part of it; the links under the settings say what they open.

**Accessibility.** Settings ▸ Accessibility: high contrast (black or white text, stronger muted text, lines and edges, links underlined), reduced motion (views stop where they are let go, pictures and cards stay still) and the size of the whole interface, 100 to 150 %. On macOS the first two follow the system's own settings unless set otherwise.

## New in 0.4.0

**Walk your map as a player.** **Player**, in 3D Sculpt, comes down into the map where the view looks, with Minecraft's body, eyes and field of view: a drag or the arrow keys look around, a click lends it the mouse as in the game (Esc gives it back), W A S D walk, Space jumps — twice quickly, flies —, Q sneaks or goes down, Shift runs, and walking into a step of one block jumps onto it. Water slows you and lets you swim; under it the world turns blue and dim. The buttons sculpt at the crosshair.

**3D Sculpt, grown up.** Sculpt, Smooth and Paint share the brush of every tool (custom images too, as set in Brush Settings); a stroke adds a layer at a time and works toward the eye at cliffs and edges. Matter pushed out keeps the blocks it came from — a sand wall gives a sand ledge, the ground under it keeps its own —, Paint repaints sculpted matter, Smooth rounds the land off without wearing it down. Brushes sculpt up to 64 blocks around in 3D.

**Noise painting.** Paint lays several terrains or blocks at once, mixed by a noise, as Axiom's noise painter does: patches, veins, blobs, cells or stripes of simplex, Perlin or value noise, with their size, detail, stretch and direction; the blocks in order, each with its share of the ground; presets, patterns saved under a name, a preview under the brush, and **Paint the whole map** in the background.

**Ground covers and custom objects.** Grass, flowers, ferns, snow or any blocks of your own, painted and grown over the ground; trees, rocks and ruins from `.schem`, `.schematic`, `.bp`, `.litematic` and `.nbt` files, imported or dropped on the window, painted where they stand.

**Automatic biomes and paint that make sense.** Sand is a desert only where sand is all around, beaches are by the water, a WorldPainter map all of one terrain is read from the shape of its land. Over the whole map they run in the background with their progress; with a brush, the land is read once a tile and kept, so brushes of any size stay quick — and no longer crash.

**Settings in four sections**: the theme and the accent colour; sounds made by Massif as they play (off, essential, or all), which leave the speakers and headphones free when silent; the system's notifications when a long task ends; a memory limit, with what is in use.

**A quieter interface.** Neutral greys and one accent, grouped controls, pill buttons, slim sliders, tool icons drawn for what they do to the land, cards with short animations, messages at the bottom right, a help page (F1). The home screen shows night scenes, dithered in a palette of their own.

**The 3D view up close.** Rivers stepping down show their falls, every block reads by its own shade and edges, deep water reflects the sky; in Slope, Height and Biome, a column's walls take its colour.

**A new README**: a banner of the home screen's night scenes, animated figures, and a guide, a page on terrain graphs and one on how Massif works, in `docs/`.

**Files.** The map is a `.massif` file's icon in the Finder and in Windows Explorer; tall WorldPainter worlds keep their height; sculpted matter keeps its blocks in the file (older files still open).

## Earlier

- **0.3.1**: a home screen; maps up to 2032 blocks tall; rivers laid out from their source, finding their own way down; a 3D Sculpt editor; height maps in and out; the node graph handled as in Gaea or Blender; a new look.
- **0.3**: rivers by hand and a Rivers node that traces them in their valleys; a Map node that reads the map you have, with the **Paint this map** and **Rivers on this map** templates; climate (temperature, humidity, biomes) and tectonic plates in the generator; terrains of any size; conversion over the map; patterns of terrains; maps of 60,000 × 50,000 blocks.
- **0.2**: export for every version from 1.7.10 to 26.3; Auto biome and Auto paint; a brush option for the way slopes face; floating islands and overhangs from the generator.
- **0.1**: the map editor — levels of rock and pits, 3D sculpting, WorldPainter's brushes and controls, the game's real blocks, the whole map in 3D, `.world` import — and the node-based terrain generator.

## Downloads

| System | File |
|---|---|
| Windows 10/11 (64-bit) | `Massif-…-windows-x86_64.zip`: unzip, run `Massif.exe` |
| macOS 11+ (Apple silicon and Intel) | `Massif-…-macos.dmg` (or `.zip`): drag Massif to Applications |
| Linux (x86-64) | `Massif-…-linux-x86_64.tar.gz`: extract, run `massif` |

The command-line tool (`massif-cli`: new, info, verify, import, export) comes with the Windows and Linux builds, and separately for macOS.

These builds are not signed by Apple or Microsoft:

- **macOS**: the first time, right-click Massif → Open, then Open again (or run `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/Massif.app`).
- **Windows**: if SmartScreen stops it, choose More info → Run anyway.

The real Minecraft blocks are read from the game installed on the computer (official launcher, CurseForge, Prism); nothing from the game is included.
